<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-projection}
For every \(X\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)\),
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf P_S(X)
  =
  \left[
  \frac{1}{m}\operatorname{Tr}_B X
  -
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{D}\mathbbm{1}_S
  \right]\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B .
  \label{eq:local-projection-formula}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Define the right-hand side of Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-projection-formula} as
\(Y\).  First,
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}_S\left[
  \frac1m\operatorname{Tr}_B X-\frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{D}\mathbbm{1}_S
  \right]
  =
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{m}
  -
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{dm}d
  =0.
\]
Therefore \(Y\in\mathcal V_S\).

Let \(A_S\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B\in\mathcal V_S\), so that \(\operatorname{Tr} A_S=0\).  Then
\begin{align}
  \langle A_S\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B,X-Y\rangle
  &=
  \frac1D
  \operatorname{Tr}\left[
  (A_S^\dagger\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B)(X-Y)
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac1D
  \operatorname{Tr}_S\left[
  A_S^\dagger\operatorname{Tr}_B(X-Y)
  \right].
  \label{eq:projection-orthogonality-step1}
\end{align}
Using Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-projection-formula},
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}_B Y
  =
  m\left[
  \frac1m\operatorname{Tr}_B X-\frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{D}\mathbbm{1}_S
  \right]
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}_B X-\frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{d}\mathbbm{1}_S.
\]
Hence
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}_B(X-Y)
  =
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{d}\mathbbm{1}_S.
\]
Substitution into Eq.~\eqref{eq:projection-orthogonality-step1} gives
\[
  \langle A_S\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B,X-Y\rangle
  =
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{dD}\operatorname{Tr} A_S^\dagger
  =0.
\]
Thus \(X-Y\) is orthogonal to \(\mathcal V_S\), while \(Y\in\mathcal V_S\).
Therefore \(Y=\mathsf P_S(X)\).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:return-matrix}
The \(q\times q\) local return matrix \(C(t)\) is defined by
\begin{equation}
  C_{ba}(t)
  :=
  \frac1d\operatorname{Tr}\left[
  P_b\Phi_t(P_a)
  \right],
  \qquad
  a,b=1,\ldots,q.
  \label{eq:return-matrix-def}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:return-overlap}
For every \(a,b\),
\begin{equation}
  C_{ba}(t)
  =
  \frac1D
  \operatorname{Tr}\left[
  O_b\,U_t O_aU_t^\dagger
  \right]
  =
  \langle O_b,\mathcal U_t(O_a)\rangle,
  \label{eq:return-matrix-overlap}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  \mathcal U_t(X):=U_tXU_t^\dagger.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By Eq.~\eqref{eq:infinite-temp-channel},
\begin{align}
  \frac1d\operatorname{Tr}_S[P_b\Phi_t(P_a)]
  &=
  \frac1d
  \operatorname{Tr}_{SB}\left[
  (P_b\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B)
  U_t
  \left(P_a\otimes\frac{\mathbbm{1}_B}{m}\right)
  U_t^\dagger
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac1{dm}
  \operatorname{Tr}_{SB}\left[
  O_bU_tO_aU_t^\dagger
  \right].
\end{align}
Since \(D=dm\), this is Eq.~\eqref{eq:return-matrix-overlap}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:traceless-expansion}
For every Hermitian \(X\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H_S)\) with \(\operatorname{Tr} X=0\),
\begin{equation}
  X
  =
  \frac1d\sum_{a=1}^q x_aP_a,
  \qquad
  x_a=\operatorname{Tr}(P_aX),
  \label{eq:traceless-expansion}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{a=1}^q x_a^2
  =
  d\,\operatorname{Tr}(X^2).
  \label{eq:parseval-system}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Because
\(\{\mathbbm{1}_S/\sqrt d,P_1/\sqrt d,\ldots,P_q/\sqrt d\}\)
is an orthonormal basis with respect to the unnormalised Hilbert--Schmidt
inner product, every \(X\) has the expansion
\[
  X
  =
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{d}\mathbbm{1}_S
  +
  \frac1d\sum_{a=1}^q\operatorname{Tr}(P_aX)P_a.
\]
The first term vanishes because \(\operatorname{Tr} X=0\), proving
Eq.~\eqref{eq:traceless-expansion}.  Squaring the expansion and using
\(\operatorname{Tr}(P_aP_b)=d\delta_{ab}\) gives
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{Tr}(X^2)
  &=
  \frac1{d^2}
  \sum_{a,b}x_ax_b\operatorname{Tr}(P_aP_b)
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac1d\sum_a x_a^2.
\end{align}
This is Eq.~\eqref{eq:parseval-system}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace-HS}
For every operator \(X\) on a \(d\)-dimensional Hilbert space,
\begin{equation}
  \left\lVertX\right\rVert_1
  \le
  \sqrt d\,\left\lVertX\right\rVert_2.
  \label{eq:trace-HS}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let \(s_1,\ldots,s_d\ge0\) be the singular values of \(X\).  Then
\[
  \left\lVertX\right\rVert_1=\sum_{j=1}^d s_j,
  \qquad
  \left\lVertX\right\rVert_2=\left(\sum_{j=1}^d s_j^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The scalar Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\[
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^d s_j\right)^2
  \le
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^d1^2\right)
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^ds_j^2\right)
  =
  d\,\left\lVertX\right\rVert_2^2.
\]
Taking square roots proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:trace-HS}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:return-controls-thermalisation}
For every Hamiltonian \(H\), every subsystem input state \(\rho_S\), and
every \(t\),
\begin{equation}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),
  \frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2
  \le
  \frac{d-1}{4}
  \left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2
  \le
  \frac{d-1}{4}
  \left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
  \label{eq:return-controls-thermalisation}
\end{equation}
Here \(\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\) and
\(\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}\) are respectively the Euclidean operator and
Frobenius norms of the \(q\times q\) matrix \(C(t)\).
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Put
\[
  \Delta
  =
  \rho_S-\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}.
\]
Then \(\Delta=\Delta^\dagger\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\Delta=0\).  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:traceless-expansion},
\begin{equation}
  \Delta
  =
  \frac1d\sum_{a=1}^q x_aP_a,
  \qquad
  x_a=\operatorname{Tr}(P_a\Delta).
  \label{eq:delta-expansion-proof}
\end{equation}
Since \(\operatorname{Tr} P_a=0\),
\[
  x_a=\operatorname{Tr}(P_a\rho_S).
\]
Again by Lemma~\ref{lem:traceless-expansion},
\begin{align}
  \left\lVertx\right\rVert_2^2
  &=
  d\,\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta^2)
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  d\operatorname{Tr}\left[
  \rho_S^2-\frac{2}{d}\rho_S+\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d^2}
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  d\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_S^2)-2+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  d\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_S^2)-1
  \nonumber\\
  &\le d-1,
  \label{eq:x-bound-proof}
\end{align}
because every density operator satisfies
\(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_S^2)\le1\).

By linearity and Eq.~\eqref{eq:maximally-mixed-fixed},
\begin{equation}
  \Phi_t(\rho_S)-\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  =
  \Phi_t(\Delta).
  \label{eq:output-difference-proof}
\end{equation}
Expand the output as
\[
  \Phi_t(\Delta)
  =
  \frac1d\sum_{b=1}^q y_bP_b.
\]
Its coefficients are
\begin{align}
  y_b
  &=
  \operatorname{Tr}[P_b\Phi_t(\Delta)]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac1d\sum_a x_a
  \operatorname{Tr}[P_b\Phi_t(P_a)]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \sum_aC_{ba}(t)x_a.
\end{align}
Thus
\begin{equation}
  y=C(t)x.
  \label{eq:y-Cx}
\end{equation}

Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-HS} and then
Lemma~\ref{lem:traceless-expansion},
\begin{align}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2
  &=
  \frac14\left\lVert\Phi_t(\Delta)\right\rVert_1^2
  \nonumber\\
  &\le
  \frac d4\left\lVert\Phi_t(\Delta)\right\rVert_2^2
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac d4
  \left(
  \frac1d\sum_b y_b^2
  \right)
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac14\left\lVerty\right\rVert_2^2
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac14\left\lVertC(t)x\right\rVert_2^2
  \nonumber\\
  &\le
  \frac14\left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2\left\lVertx\right\rVert_2^2
  \nonumber\\
  &\le
  \frac{d-1}{4}
  \left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2.
\end{align}
Finally,
\(\left\lVertC\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le\left\lVertC\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}\),
because the largest singular value is no larger than the square root of
the sum of squared singular values.  This proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:return-controls-thermalisation}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The quantity
\[
  \frac{1}{d^2-1}\left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2
\]
is the unitarity of the traceless block of the reduced channel in the
standard channel-transfer-matrix terminology; see
Ref.~\cite{WallmanGranadeHarperFlammia2015}.  Here it is interpreted
dynamically as the mean return of a complete local operator basis.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:manybody-return}
Define
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf K_S(t)
  :=
  \mathsf P_S\mathcal U_t\mathsf P_S
  :
  \mathcal V_S\longrightarrow\mathcal V_S.
  \label{eq:manybody-return}
\end{equation}
Its squared Hilbert--Schmidt norm, which sums the return over all
\(q\) basis directions, is
\begin{equation}
  R_S(t)
  :=
  \left\lVert\mathsf K_S(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
  \label{eq:return-probability}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:return-equals-C}
For every \(t\),
\begin{equation}
  R_S(t)=\left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
  \label{eq:return-equals-C}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
In the orthonormal basis \(\{O_a\}_{a=1}^q\) of \(\mathcal V_S\), the matrix
entries of \(\mathsf K_S(t)\) are
\begin{align}
  \langle O_b,\mathsf K_S(t)O_a\rangle
  &=
  \langle O_b,\mathsf P_S\mathcal U_tO_a\rangle
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \langle \mathsf P_SO_b,\mathcal U_tO_a\rangle
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \langle O_b,\mathcal U_tO_a\rangle
  =
  C_{ba}(t),
\end{align}
where we used \(\mathsf P_SO_b=O_b\) and
Lemma~\ref{lem:return-overlap}.  The squared Frobenius norm is the sum of
the squared moduli of the matrix entries, hence
\[
  R_S(t)
  =
  \sum_{a,b=1}^q\left\lvertC_{ba}(t)\right\rvert^2
  =
  \left\lVertC(t)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Cesaro-orthogonality}
For real numbers \(\omega,\nu\),
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{T\to\infty}
  \frac1T\int_0^T
  e^{it(\omega-\nu)}\,dt
  =
  \begin{cases}
  1,&\omega=\nu,\\
  0,&\omega\ne\nu.
  \end{cases}
  \label{eq:Cesaro-orthogonality}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If \(\omega=\nu\), the integrand is \(1\), and the average equals \(1\).
If \(\omega\ne\nu\), direct integration gives
\[
  \frac1T\int_0^T
  e^{it(\omega-\nu)}dt
  =
  \frac{e^{iT(\omega-\nu)}-1}
  {iT(\omega-\nu)}.
\]
The numerator has absolute value at most \(2\), while the denominator has
absolute value \(T\left\lvert\omega-\nu\right\rvert\).  The ratio therefore converges to
zero.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:exact-return-spectral}
The infinite-time average of the total local return is
\begin{equation}
  \overline{R_S(t)}
  =
  \sum_\omega
  \left\lVert
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega\mathsf P_S
  \right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
  \label{eq:exact-return-spectral}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, in the basis \(\{O_a\}\),
\begin{equation}
  \overline{R_S(t)}
  =
  \sum_{a,b=1}^q
  \sum_\omega
  \left\lvert
  \langle O_b,\mathsf Q_\omega O_a\rangle
  \right\rvert^2.
  \label{eq:exact-return-spectral-components}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By Definition~\ref{def:manybody-return},
\[
  R_S(t)
  =
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_S\mathcal U_t\mathsf P_S\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
\]
For a finite-dimensional operator \(A\),
\(\left\lVertA\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}(A^\dagger A)\), where the trace is
over operator Hilbert space.  Hence
\begin{align}
  R_S(t)
  &=
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}\left[
  \mathsf P_S
  \mathcal U_t^\dagger
  \mathsf P_S
  \mathcal U_t
  \mathsf P_S
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \sum_{\omega,\nu}
  e^{it(\omega-\nu)}
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}\left[
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\nu
  \mathsf P_S
  \right],
  \label{eq:return-before-Cesaro}
\end{align}
where Eq.~\eqref{eq:Liouvillian-time-evolution} was used.

Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:Cesaro-orthogonality} term by term leaves only
\(\omega=\nu\):
\begin{align}
  \overline{R_S(t)}
  &=
  \sum_\omega
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}\left[
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega
  \mathsf P_S
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \sum_\omega
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}\left[
  (\mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega\mathsf P_S)^2
  \right].
\end{align}
The operator
\(\mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega\mathsf P_S\) is self-adjoint, so its squared
Frobenius norm equals the last trace.  This proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:exact-return-spectral}.

To obtain Eq.~\eqref{eq:exact-return-spectral-components}, use the
orthonormal basis \(\{O_a\}\) of \(\mathcal V_S\).  For each \(\omega\),
\[
  \left\lVert
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_\omega\mathsf P_S
  \right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2
  =
  \sum_{a,b}
  \left\lvert
  \langle O_b,\mathsf Q_\omega O_a\rangle
  \right\rvert^2.
\]
Summing over \(\omega\) proves the result.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:tent-domination}
Fix \(T>0\), \(t_0\in\mathbb R\), and put
\[
  c=t_0+\frac T2,
  \qquad
  w_T(t)
  =
  \left(
  1-\frac{|t-c|}{T}
  \right)_+.
\]
For every nonnegative measurable \(f\),
\begin{equation}
  \frac1T\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}f(t)\,dt
  \le
  \frac2T\int_{\mathbb R}w_T(t)f(t)\,dt.
  \label{eq:tent-domination}
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every real \(\Delta\),
\begin{equation}
  \frac1T
  \int_{\mathbb R}
  w_T(t)e^{it\Delta}\,dt
  =
  e^{ic\Delta}
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T\Delta}{2}
  \right),
  \label{eq:tent-fourier}
\end{equation}
where \(\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1\) and
\(\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin x/x\) for \(x\ne0\).
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For \(t\in[t_0,t_0+T]\),
\[
  |t-c|\le\frac T2,
\]
so \(w_T(t)\ge1/2\).  Hence
\[
  \mathbbm 1_{[t_0,t_0+T]}(t)
  \le2w_T(t),
\]
which proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:tent-domination} after multiplication by
\(f(t)\ge0\) and integration.

For the Fourier transform, substitute \(s=t-c\).  Then
\begin{align}
  &\frac1T
  \int_{\mathbb R}
  w_T(t)e^{it\Delta}\,dt
  \nonumber\\
  &\quad=
  \frac{e^{ic\Delta}}{T}
  \int_{-T}^{T}
  \left(
  1-\frac{|s|}{T}
  \right)e^{is\Delta}\,ds
  \nonumber\\
  &\quad=
  \frac{2e^{ic\Delta}}{T}
  \int_0^T
  \left(
  1-\frac{s}{T}
  \right)\cos(s\Delta)\,ds.
  \label{eq:tent-transform-step}
\end{align}
If \(\Delta\ne0\), direct integration gives
\[
  2\int_0^T
  \left(
  1-\frac{s}{T}
  \right)\cos(s\Delta)\,ds
  =
  T\left[
  \frac{\sin(T\Delta/2)}{T\Delta/2}
  \right]^2.
\]
The identity extends continuously to \(\Delta=0\), proving
Eq.~\eqref{eq:tent-fourier}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-spectral-weights-new}
The probability measure \(\mu_S\) is supported in
\([-2\left\lVertH\right\rVert_\infty,2\left\lVertH\right\rVert_\infty]\).  Moreover, for all
Liouvillian frequencies \(\omega,\nu\),
\begin{equation}
  0
  \le
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}(A_\omega A_\nu)
  \le
  q^2\pi_\omega\pi_\nu.
  \label{eq:local-cross-new}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For \(X\in\mathcal V_S\),
\[
  \langle X,A_\omega X\rangle
  =
  \langle X,\mathsf Q_\omega X\rangle
  =
  \left\lVert\mathsf Q_\omega X\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  \ge0,
\]
so \(A_\omega\ge0\) and \(\pi_\omega\ge0\).  Since
\[
  \sum_\omega A_\omega=\mathsf P_S
\]
and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}\mathsf P_S=q\),
\[
  \sum_\omega\pi_\omega=1.
\]
Every Liouvillian frequency is an energy difference and therefore has
absolute value at most \(2\left\lVertH\right\rVert_\infty\).

For positive operators \(A,B\), one has
\[
  A\le(\operatorname{Tr} A)\mathbbm{1}
\]
because every eigenvalue of \(A\) is nonnegative and no eigenvalue exceeds
their sum.  Thus
\[
  0\le\operatorname{Tr}(AB)\le(\operatorname{Tr} A)(\operatorname{Tr} B).
\]
Apply this to \(A_\omega,A_\nu\) and use
\(\operatorname{Tr} A_\omega=q\pi_\omega\).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:fejer-local-band}
For every Hamiltonian \(H\), every
\(t_0,T,\varepsilon>0\), and every local input state,
\begin{align}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  R_S(t)\,dt
  &\le
  4q^2\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)
  \left[
  1+
  \frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\varepsilon)^2}
  \right],
  \label{eq:fejer-local-return}\\
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2dt
  &\le
  (d-1)q^2\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)
  \left[
  1+
  \frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\varepsilon)^2}
  \right].
  \label{eq:fejer-local-trace}
\end{align}
No nondegeneracy assumption on energies or gaps is required.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The exact Liouvillian expansion gives
\[
  \mathsf K_S(t)
  =
  \sum_\omega e^{-it\omega}A_\omega
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}
  R_S(t)
  =
  \sum_{\omega,\nu}
  e^{it(\omega-\nu)}
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}(A_\omega A_\nu).
  \label{eq:local-return-spectrum-new}
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:tent-domination} and nonnegativity of \(R_S(t)\),
the rectangular average is no larger than twice its tent-weighted
average.  Using Eq.~\eqref{eq:tent-fourier},
Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-return-spectrum-new}, and
Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-cross-new} gives
\begin{align}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}R_S(t)dt
  &\le
  2q^2
  \sum_{\omega,\nu}
  \pi_\omega\pi_\nu
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right).
  \label{eq:local-fejer-double}
\end{align}
Fix \(\omega\).  The region
\[
  |\omega-\nu|<\varepsilon
\]
is covered by two intervals of width \(\varepsilon\), so its
\(\mu_S\)-mass is at most \(2\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)\).  For each
integer \(\ell\ge1\), the shell
\[
  \ell\varepsilon
  \le
  |\omega-\nu|
  <
  (\ell+1)\varepsilon
\]
has mass at most \(2\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)\), while
Eq.~\eqref{eq:sinc-square-bound} gives
\[
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right)
  \le
  \frac4{T^2\ell^2\varepsilon^2}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align}
  \sum_\nu
  \pi_\nu
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right)
  &\le
  2\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)
  \left[
  1+
  \frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\varepsilon)^2}
  \right].
  \label{eq:local-fejer-fixedomega}
\end{align}
Average over \(\omega\) with total weight one and substitute into
Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-fejer-double}.  This proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:fejer-local-return}.  Equation
\eqref{eq:trace-distance-by-return-probability} then gives
Eq.~\eqref{eq:fejer-local-trace}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:no-time-resolution-overhead}
For every \(T>0\),
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t_0,\rho_S}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2dt
  \le
  C_d\,
  \chi_S(T^{-1};H),
  \label{eq:no-time-resolution-overhead}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  C_d
  =
  (d-1)(d^2-1)^2
  \left(
  1+\frac{2\pi^2}{3}
  \right).
\]
Consequently, if a fixed subsystem satisfies
\[
  \chi_S(N^{-c};H_N)=O(N^{-\kappa}),
\]
then windows \(T_N=N^c\) already give
\[
  \sup_{t_0,\rho_S}
  \frac1{T_N}\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T_N}D_{\rm tr}^2dt
  =
  O_S(N^{-\kappa}).
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Set \(\varepsilon=T^{-1}\) in
Theorem~\ref{thm:fejer-local-band}.  Then \(T\varepsilon=1\).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:temporal-transfer}
On the traceless local operator space, the transfer matrix of
\(\overline{\Phi}\) is \(A_0\).  The transfer matrix of
\(\Phi_t-\overline{\Phi}\) is
\(\widetilde{\mathsf K}_S(t)\).
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
In the orthonormal basis \(\{O_a\}\) of \(\mathcal V_S\), the transfer matrix
of \(\Phi_t\) is the matrix of
\[
  \mathsf K_S(t)
  =
  \sum_\omega e^{-it\omega}A_\omega
\]
by Proposition~\ref{prop:return-equals-C}.  Ces\`aro orthogonality,
Lemma~\ref{lem:Cesaro-orthogonality}, removes every term with
\(\omega\ne0\), leaving \(A_0\).  Subtracting the temporal transfer
matrix from the time-\(t\) transfer matrix leaves
\(\widetilde{\mathsf K}_S(t)\).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:separated-stationary}
For every local input state,
\begin{equation}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2
  \le
  \frac{d-1}{4}q^2\pi_{0,S}^2.
  \label{eq:separated-stationary}
\end{equation}
Thus exact conserved local memory enters quadratically in the
mean-square trace-distance error.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Repeat the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:return-controls-thermalisation}, replacing the transfer
matrix \(C(t)\) by the temporal transfer matrix \(A_0\) from
Lemma~\ref{lem:temporal-transfer}.  This gives
\[
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2
  \le
  \frac{d-1}{4}\left\lVertA_0\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
\]
Since \(A_0\ge0\),
\[
  \left\lVertA_0\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2
  =
  \sum_j\lambda_j(A_0)^2
  \le
  \left(
  \sum_j\lambda_j(A_0)
  \right)^2
  =
  (\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}A_0)^2
  =
  q^2\pi_{0,S}^2.
\]
Substitution proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:separated-window}
For every \(t_0,T,\varepsilon>0\) and every local input state,
\begin{align}
  &\frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S)
  \right)^2dt
  \nonumber\\
  &\quad\le
  (d-1)q^2
  m_S
  \widetilde\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)
  \left[
  1+
  \frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\varepsilon)^2}
  \right],
  \label{eq:separated-fluctuation}
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
  &\frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2dt
  \nonumber\\
  &\quad\le
  \frac{d-1}{2}q^2\pi_{0,S}^2
  +
  2(d-1)q^2
  m_S
  \widetilde\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)
  \left[
  1+
  \frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\varepsilon)^2}
  \right].
  \label{eq:separated-total}
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:temporal-transfer}, the traceless transfer block of
\(\Phi_t-\overline{\Phi}\) is
\(\widetilde{\mathsf K}_S(t)\).  The norm conversion in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:return-controls-thermalisation} therefore gives
\begin{equation}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S)
  \right)^2
  \le
  \frac{d-1}{4}
  \left\lVert
  \widetilde{\mathsf K}_S(t)
  \right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2.
  \label{eq:fluctuation-pointwise}
\end{equation}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tent-domination} to the nonnegative right-hand side.
The same spectral calculation as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:fejer-local-band}, but summing only over
\(\omega,\nu\ne0\), yields
\begin{align}
  &\frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  \left\lVert
  \widetilde{\mathsf K}_S(t)
  \right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2dt
  \nonumber\\
  &\quad\le
  4q^2m_S\widetilde\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)
  \left[
  1+
  \frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\varepsilon)^2}
  \right].
  \label{eq:tilde-K-window}
\end{align}
Indeed, for fixed nonzero \(\omega\), every central region or shell has
\(\widetilde\mu_S\)-mass at most
\(2\widetilde\chi_S(\varepsilon;H)\), and integration over the first
frequency has total mass \(m_S\).  Combining
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:fluctuation-pointwise} and
\eqref{eq:tilde-K-window} proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:separated-fluctuation}.

For the total error, the trace-distance triangle inequality gives
\[
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)
  \le
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S)
  \right)
  +
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right).
\]
Using
\[
  (a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2,
\]
averaging, applying
Eq.~\eqref{eq:separated-fluctuation} to the first term and
Theorem~\ref{thm:separated-stationary} to the second proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:separated-total}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:separated-same-scale}
Setting \(\varepsilon=T^{-1}\) gives
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t_0,\rho_S}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2dt
  \le
  C_d
  \left[
  \pi_{0,S}^2+
  \widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H)
  \right]
  \label{eq:separated-same-scale}
\end{equation}
for a constant \(C_d\) depending only on the subsystem dimension.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Use \(m_S\le1\) and \(T\varepsilon=1\) in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:separated-total}, and absorb the fixed numerical factors
into \(C_d\).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:phi-autocorr-new}
Equations~\eqref{eq:phi-local-new} and
\eqref{eq:phi-basis-new} hold, and
\begin{equation}
  A_S^{\rm F}(T)
  =
  \iint
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right)
  \widetilde\mu_S(d\omega)
  \widetilde\mu_S(d\nu).
  \label{eq:AF-convolution-new}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The spectral theorem gives
\[
  e^{-it\mathcal L}
  =
  \sum_\omega e^{-it\omega}\mathsf Q_\omega.
\]
Taking the operator-space trace after compression by \(\mathsf P_S\)
gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:phi-local-new}; evaluating that trace in the
orthonormal basis \(\{O_a\}\) gives
Eq.~\eqref{eq:phi-basis-new}.

Next,
\[
  |\widetilde\varphi_S(t)|^2
  =
  \iint
  e^{-it(\omega-\nu)}
  \widetilde\mu_S(d\omega)
  \widetilde\mu_S(d\nu).
\]
The measure is finite and the integrand is bounded, so Fubini's theorem
applies.  Equation~\eqref{eq:tent-fourier} with centre zero gives
Eq.~\eqref{eq:AF-convolution-new}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:same-scale-equivalence-new}
Let
\[
  c_*
  =
  \frac{\sin(1/2)}{1/2}.
\]
For every \(T>0\),
\begin{equation}
  \frac{c_*^2}{2}
  \widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H)^2
  \le
  A_S(T)
  \le
  4m_S
  \left(
  1+\frac{2\pi^2}{3}
  \right)
  \widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H).
  \label{eq:same-scale-equivalence-new}
\end{equation}
There is no logarithmic loss and no change of time scale.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let \(I\) be an interval of length \(1/T\).  If
\(\omega,\nu\in I\), then
\[
  \left|
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right|
  \le\frac12.
\]
The function \(\operatorname{sinc}(x)\) is even and decreasing on
\([0,1/2]\), so
\[
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right)
  \ge c_*^2.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:AF-convolution-new} therefore gives
\[
  A_S^{\rm F}(T)
  \ge
  c_*^2\,\widetilde\mu_S(I)^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(I\),
\begin{equation}
  A_S^{\rm F}(T)
  \ge
  c_*^2
  \widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H)^2.
  \label{eq:AF-lower-new}
\end{equation}
Since the triangular weight is at most one,
\[
  A_S^{\rm F}(T)
  \le
  \frac1T
  \int_{-T}^{T}
  |\widetilde\varphi_S(t)|^2dt
  =
  2A_S(T).
\]
This proves the lower inequality.

For the upper inequality, fix \(\omega\).  The same shell decomposition as
in Theorem~\ref{thm:fejer-local-band}, now for
\(\widetilde\mu_S\) and with \(\varepsilon=T^{-1}\), gives
\begin{align}
  &\int
  \operatorname{sinc}^2
  \left(
  \frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2
  \right)
  \widetilde\mu_S(d\nu)
  \nonumber\\
  &\qquad\le
  2\widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H)
  \left(
  1+\frac{2\pi^2}{3}
  \right).
  \label{eq:AF-upper-fixed-new}
\end{align}
Integrating over \(\omega\), whose total
\(\widetilde\mu_S\)-mass is \(m_S\), gives
\begin{equation}
  A_S^{\rm F}(T)
  \le
  2m_S
  \left(
  1+\frac{2\pi^2}{3}
  \right)
  \widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H).
  \label{eq:AF-upper-new}
\end{equation}
Apply this at time \(2T\).  For \(|t|\le T\),
\[
  1-\frac{|t|}{2T}\ge\frac12,
\]
so
\[
  A_S^{\rm F}(2T)
  \ge
  \frac1{4T}
  \int_{-T}^{T}
  |\widetilde\varphi_S(t)|^2dt
  =
  \frac12A_S(T).
\]
Consequently
\[
  A_S(T)
  \le
  2A_S^{\rm F}(2T)
  \le
  4m_S
  \left(
  1+\frac{2\pi^2}{3}
  \right)
  \widetilde\chi_S((2T)^{-1};H).
\]
The concentration function is nondecreasing in interval width, hence
\[
  \widetilde\chi_S((2T)^{-1};H)
  \le
  \widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H).
\]
This proves the upper inequality.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{eq:same-scale-equivalence-new} gives
\(\widetilde\chi_S(T^{-1};H)\le\sqrt{2A_S(T)}/c_*\).
A linear bound of a maximum cell mass by this mean square is false for
general positive measures.  For example, fix \(0<p<1/2\), put
\(M=\lceil p^{-2}\rceil\), and use
\[
 \mu_p=p\delta_{2\pi}+\frac{1-p}{M}
                   \sum_{j=2}^{M+1}\delta_{2\pi j}.
\]
All atoms are nonzero, every unit-width interval contains at most one,
and \((1-p)/M\le p^2<p\); thus its unit-width concentration equals \(p\).
At \(T=1\), exact integration of the distinct integer-frequency
exponentials gives
\[
 \frac12\int_{-1}^{1}|\widehat\mu_p(t)|^2dt
 =p^2+\frac{(1-p)^2}{M}\le2p^2.
\]
The ratio of concentration to mean square is therefore at least
\(1/(2p)\), which is unbounded as \(p\downarrow0\).
This is a measure-theoretic obstruction to that \emph{intermediate}
inference, not a lower bound on physical local relaxation.
The next theorem avoids the inference entirely.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:window-measurability}
For fixed \(T>0\), \(\mathscr E_H(T)\) and \(\mathscr G_H(T)\) are Borel
functions of a finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix \(H\).  They take values
in \([0,1]\).
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The exponential \(e^{-itH}\) is continuous in \(t\) and the matrix entries
of \(H\).  The density-operator set is compact.  Consequently the
supremum defining \(e_H(t)\) is continuous in \((H,t)\): a convergent
sequence of \((H,t)\)'s gives uniform convergence over this compact input
set.  Its average over a window is continuous in \((H,t_0)\).
The supremum over \(t_0\ge0\) equals the supremum over nonnegative rational
\(t_0\), by continuity in \(t_0\); a countable supremum of continuous
functions is Borel.

Every matrix entry of \(\overline\Phi\) is a pointwise limit of finite-time
averages of continuous functions of \(H\), hence is Borel.  For fixed
\(H\), both the input and time dependence of the expression defining
\(f_H(t)\) are continuous.  Its input supremum can be taken over a
countable dense subset of density operators.  It is therefore Borel in
\((H,t)\); its bounded time integral is Borel in \((H,t_0)\).
Taking the supremum over rational starting times proves the second
measurability assertion.  Trace distance between two states is at most
one, which proves the range assertion.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:positive-kernel-return}
For every finite Hamiltonian, every subsystem of dimension \(d\ge2\), and
every \(T>0\),
\begin{align}
 \mathscr E_H(T)
     \le \mathfrak c_d\,\mathcal F_S(T;H)
     \le 2\mathfrak c_d\,\mathcal A_S(T;H),
 \label{eq:positive-kernel-full}\\
 \mathscr G_H(T)
     \le \mathfrak c_d\,A_S^{\rm F}(T)
     \le 2\mathfrak c_d\,A_S(T).
 \label{eq:positive-kernel-fluct}
\end{align}
No spectral nondegeneracy, locality, or randomness assumption is needed.
The right-hand sides involve correlations only on \([-T,T]\), although
the bounds hold simultaneously in every translated window.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let \(\Omega_*\) be either the entire set of Liouvillian frequencies or
the same set with zero removed.  Put
\[
 K_*(t)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_*}e^{-it\omega}A_\omega,\qquad
 R_*(t)=\|K_*(t)\|_{\mathrm F}^2,\qquad
 \mu_*=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_*}\pi_\omega\delta_\omega.
\]
The definitions in the finite-window section give
\(A_\omega\ge0\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}A_\omega=q\pi_\omega\).
For
\[
 a_{\omega\nu}=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}(A_\omega A_\nu),
\]
positivity implies
\[
 0\le a_{\omega\nu}\le q^2\pi_\omega\pi_\nu.
\]
Indeed, the first inequality follows by taking the trace of
\(A_\nu^{1/2}A_\omega A_\nu^{1/2}\), and the second follows from
\(A_\omega\le(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}A_\omega)\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal V_S}\).
Finite expansion of the squared norm gives
\[
 R_*(t)=\sum_{\omega,\nu\in\Omega_*}
           e^{it(\omega-\nu)}a_{\omega\nu}.
\]

Fix \(t_0\ge0\), write \(c=t_0+T/2\), and use the tent
\(w(t)=(1-|t-c|/T)_+\) from Lemma~\ref{lem:tent-domination}.
Since \(R_*(t)\ge0\),
\begin{align}
 \frac1T\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}R_*(t)dt
 &\le \frac2T\int_{\mathbb R}w(t)R_*(t)dt \nonumber\\
 &=2\sum_{\omega,\nu\in\Omega_*}
      a_{\omega\nu}e^{ic(\omega-\nu)}
       \operatorname{sinc}^2\!\left(\frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2\right)
       \nonumber\\
 &\le 2q^2\sum_{\omega,\nu\in\Omega_*}
      \pi_\omega\pi_\nu
       \operatorname{sinc}^2\!\left(\frac{T(\omega-\nu)}2\right).
 \label{eq:positive-kernel-spectral}
\end{align}
For the final inequality take the absolute value of the preceding finite
sum.  Every sinc-squared factor and every \(a_{\omega\nu}\) is
nonnegative, so removing the phase can only increase this upper bound.

By the tent Fourier identity, the last sum is
\[
 \frac{2q^2}{T}\int_{-T}^{T}
       \left(1-\frac{|t|}{T}\right)|\widehat\mu_*(t)|^2dt.
\]
For the full frequency set, the pointwise return theorem gives
\(e_H(t)\le(d-1)R_*(t)/4\); for the nonzero frequency set,
Eq.~\eqref{eq:fluctuation-pointwise} gives the same bound for \(f_H(t)\).
Both pointwise bounds hold for every input, so taking its supremum before
integration is legitimate.  Multiplication by \((d-1)/4\), followed by
the supremum over \(t_0\), proves the first inequalities in
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:positive-kernel-full} and
\eqref{eq:positive-kernel-fluct}.
The triangular weight is at most one, so its normalized integral is at
most twice the corresponding rectangular average.  This proves the
remaining inequalities.  The use of negative times in the auxiliary
integral is harmless: \(e^{-itH}\) is defined for every real \(t\).
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:linear-dynamical-equivalence}
For the same hypotheses,
\begin{align}
 \frac{\mathcal A_S(T;H)}{4d^2}
 &\le \mathscr E_H(T)
 \le (d-1)q^2\,\mathcal A_S(T;H),\\
 \frac{A_S(T)}{4d^2}
 &\le \mathscr G_H(T)
 \le (d-1)q^2\,A_S(T).
 \label{eq:linear-dynamical-equivalence}
\end{align}
Thus at fixed subsystem dimension the correlation mean square and the
every-window local error are comparable \emph{linearly}.  The nonlinear
conversion in the concentration theorem is not a dynamical necessity.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Only the lower bounds remain to be proved.  Choose the Hermitian basis
\(P_a\) used in Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-operator-basis}, let
\(p_a=\|P_a\|_\infty\), and define
\[
 \rho_a=\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S+P_a/p_a}{d}.
\]
Here \(p_a>0\), every eigenvalue of \(P_a/p_a\) is at least \(-1\), and
\(\operatorname{Tr} P_a=0\).  Thus \(\rho_a\) is a state.  Also
\(p_a^2\le\operatorname{Tr} P_a^2=d\).

Let \(\Lambda_t\) denote either the map
\(X\mapsto\Phi_t(X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X)\mathbbm{1}_S/d\), or
\(\Phi_t-\overline\Phi\).  In either case
\(\Lambda_t(\mathbbm{1}_S)=0\), and its traceless transfer matrix \(C_*(t)\)
is respectively the matrix of \(\mathsf K_S(t)\) or of
\(\widetilde{\mathsf K}_S(t)\).
The expansion
\(\Lambda_t(P_a)=\sum_b(C_*(t))_{ba}P_b\) gives
\[
 \|\Lambda_t(\rho_a)\|_2^2
 =\frac1{d p_a^2}\sum_b|(C_*(t))_{ba}|^2.
\]
For singular values, the sum of squares does not exceed the square of
the sum, so \(\|X\|_1\ge\|X\|_2\).  Therefore the appropriate squared
trace-distance error for input \(\rho_a\) is at least
\[
 \frac1{4d^2}\sum_b|(C_*(t))_{ba}|^2.
\]
Summing this inequality over \(a\) and using the worst-input supremum gives
\(R_*(t)\le4d^2q\,e_H(t)\), or the same inequality with \(f_H(t)\).

Finally,
\[
 |\widehat\mu_*(t)|^2
 =q^{-2}|\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}K_*(t)|^2
 \le q^{-1}R_*(t)
\]
by the scalar Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied to its diagonal matrix
entries.  Since \(K_*(-t)=K_*(t)^\dagger\), both \(R_*(t)\) and
\(|\widehat\mu_*(t)|^2\) are even.  Hence their average on \([-T,T]\)
equals their average on \([0,T]\).  Combining the last two bounds and
using the window with \(t_0=0\) proves both lower bounds.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:direct-from-autocorrelation-new}
For every \(T>0\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E_H(T)
 \le \mathfrak c_d\left[\pi_{0,S}^2+2A_S^{\rm F}(T)\right]
 \le \mathfrak c_d\left[\pi_{0,S}^2+4A_S(T)\right].
 \label{eq:direct-from-autocorrelation-new}
\end{equation}
The dependence on the correlation mean square is linear.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The trace-distance triangle inequality and
\((x+y)^2\le2x^2+2y^2\) bound \(e_H(t)\) by twice \(f_H(t)\)
plus twice the worst stationary error.  The stationary error is at most
\((d-1)q^2\pi_{0,S}^2/4\) by
Theorem~\ref{thm:separated-stationary}.  Now apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-kernel-return} to the time average of
\(f_H(t)\), and use \(A_S^{\rm F}(T)\le2A_S(T)\).
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:linear-annealed}
For any random Hamiltonian ensemble, if
\(\mathbb E A_S(T)\le a\) and
\(\mathbb E\pi_{0,S}^2\le p_2\), then
\[
 \mathbb E\mathscr E_H(T)\le\mathfrak c_d(p_2+4a),\qquad
 \mathbb P[\mathscr E_H(T)>u]
 \le \frac{\mathfrak c_d(p_2+4a)}{u}\quad(u>0).
\]
The event concerns all starting times and all subsystem inputs
simultaneously.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Take expectations in Eq.~\eqref{eq:direct-from-autocorrelation-new}.
Measurability follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:window-measurability}.
For a nonnegative random variable \(X\),
\(X\ge u\,\mathbbm1_{\{X>u\}}\), so
\(\mathbb P[X>u]\le\mathbb EX/u\).  Apply this with
\(X=\mathscr E_H(T)\).
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:pi0-energy-lower}
Let
\[
  \widetilde H
  =
  H-\frac{\operatorname{Tr} H}{D}\mathbbm{1}.
\]
If \(\widetilde H\ne0\), then
\begin{equation}
  \pi_{0,S}
  \ge
  \frac1q
  \frac{
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_S\widetilde H\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  }{
  \left\lVert\widetilde H\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  },
  \qquad
  q=d^2-1.
  \label{eq:pi0-energy-lower}
\end{equation}
If \(\widetilde H=0\), the right-hand side is defined as zero and the
inequality remains valid.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Suppose first that \(\widetilde H\ne0\) and set
\[
  X_H
  =
  \frac{\widetilde H}{\left\lVert\widetilde H\right\rVert_{2,D}}.
\]
Since \([H,\widetilde H]=0\), one has
\(X_H\in\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf Q_0\), and
\(\left\lVertX_H\right\rVert_{2,D}=1\).
Extend \(X_H\) to an orthonormal basis
\(\{X_j\}\) of \(\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf Q_0\).  Then
\begin{align}
  q\pi_{0,S}
  &=
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}
  \left[
  \mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_0\mathsf P_S
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal K}
  \left[
  \mathsf Q_0\mathsf P_S\mathsf Q_0
  \right]
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \sum_j
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_SX_j\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  \nonumber\\
  &\ge
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_SX_H\right\rVert_{2,D}^2.
\end{align}
Substituting the definition of \(X_H\) proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:pi0-energy-lower}.  If
\(\widetilde H=0\), the declared right-hand side is zero while
\(\pi_{0,S}\ge0\).
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:HN-HS-upper}
For the ensemble
Eq.~\eqref{eq:Haar-local-floor-ensemble} under
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:local-traceless-floor} and
\eqref{eq:local-norm-floor}, there is a constant
\[
  C_H=C_H(k,\Delta,c_E,J)
\]
independent of \(N\) and of the Haar realization such that
\begin{equation}
  \left\lVertH_N\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  \le
  C_HN.
  \label{eq:HN-HS-upper}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Expand
\[
  \left\lVertH_N\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  =
  \sum_{X,Y\in\mathcal E_N}
  \langle h_X,h_Y\rangle.
\]
If \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\), then the normalized trace factorizes:
\[
  \langle h_X,h_Y\rangle
  =
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr}_Xh_X}{d_X}
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr}_Yh_Y}{d_Y}
  =
  0
\]
by Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-traceless-floor}.
For arbitrary \(X,Y\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
  |\langle h_X,h_Y\rangle|
  \le
  \left\lVerth_X\right\rVert_{2,D}
  \left\lVerth_Y\right\rVert_{2,D}.
\]
Because \(h_X\) acts nontrivially only on \(X\),
\[
  \left\lVerth_X\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  =
  \frac1{d_X}\operatorname{Tr}_X(h_X^2)
  \le
  \left\lVerth_X\right\rVert_\infty^2
  =
  \left\lVert\Lambda_X\right\rVert_\infty^2
  \le
  J^2.
\]
Thus every nonzero summand has modulus at most \(J^2\).

Fix \(X\).  Since \(|X|\le k\) and every site belongs to at most
\(\Delta\) interaction supports, the number of \(Y\) with
\(Y\cap X\ne\varnothing\) is at most \(k\Delta\).  Hence the number of
ordered pairs \((X,Y)\) that can contribute is at most
\[
  |\mathcal E_N|\,k\Delta
  \le
  c_Ek\Delta\,N.
\]
Therefore
\[
  \left\lVertH_N\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  \le
  c_Ek\Delta J^2\,N.
\]
One may take
\[
  C_H=c_Ek\Delta J^2.
\]
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:Haar-local-pi0-floor}
Fix a subsystem \(S\), independent of \(N\), and suppose it contains one
interaction support \(X_0\in\mathcal E_N\).  Assume
\begin{equation}
  v_{X_0}
  :=
  \frac1{d_{X_0}}
  \operatorname{Tr}_{X_0}(\Lambda_{X_0}^2)
  \ge v_*>0
  \label{eq:vstar-floor}
\end{equation}
uniformly in \(N\).  Then
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb E\,\pi_{0,S}
  \ge
  \frac{v_*}{qC_H}\frac1N.
  \label{eq:Haar-local-pi0-floor}
\end{equation}
Thus, for the unseparated local concentration
\(\chi_S\) defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-chi-new},
\[
  \mathbb E\,\chi_S(\varepsilon;H_N)
  \ge
  \frac{v_*}{qC_H}\frac1N
\]
for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
By Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-traceless-floor},
\[
  \operatorname{Tr} H_N=0,
\]
so \(\widetilde H_N=H_N\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi0-energy-lower} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:HN-HS-upper} give pointwise
\begin{equation}
  \pi_{0,S}
  \ge
  \frac{
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_SH_N\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  }{
  qC_HN
  }.
  \label{eq:pi0-floor-pointwise}
\end{equation}
It remains to lower-bound the expectation of the numerator.

Linearity of \(\mathsf P_S\) gives
\[
  \mathsf P_SH_N
  =
  \sum_X\mathsf P_Sh_X.
\]
For each traceless \(\Lambda_X\), Haar invariance implies
\[
  \mathbb E\,h_X
  =
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr}_X\Lambda_X}{d_X}\mathbbm{1}_X
  =
  0.
\]
The \(U_X\) are independent.  Hence for \(X\ne Y\),
conditioning on all variables except \(U_X\) gives
\[
  \mathbb E
  \langle
  \mathsf P_Sh_X,\mathsf P_Sh_Y
  \rangle
  =
  0.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align}
  \mathbb E
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_SH_N\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  &=
  \sum_X
  \mathbb E
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_Sh_X\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  \nonumber\\
  &\ge
  \mathbb E
  \left\lVert\mathsf P_Sh_{X_0}\right\rVert_{2,D}^2.
  \label{eq:local-projection-expectation}
\end{align}
Because \(X_0\subseteq S\) and \(h_{X_0}\) is traceless,
\(h_{X_0}\), embedded by identities outside \(X_0\), belongs to
\(\mathcal V_S\).  Hence
\[
  \mathsf P_Sh_{X_0}=h_{X_0}
\]
and
\[
  \left\lVerth_{X_0}\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  =
  \frac1{d_{X_0}}
  \operatorname{Tr}_{X_0}(h_{X_0}^2)
  =
  \frac1{d_{X_0}}
  \operatorname{Tr}_{X_0}(\Lambda_{X_0}^2)
  =
  v_{X_0}
  \ge
  v_*.
\]
Taking expectations in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:pi0-floor-pointwise} and using
Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-projection-expectation} proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:Haar-local-pi0-floor}.

Finally every interval containing zero has
\[
  \chi_S(\varepsilon;H_N)\ge\pi_{0,S},
\]
so the same expectation lower bound holds for \(\chi_S\).
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The theorem explains why the zero mode must be separated before asking
for fast dynamical spectral spreading.  The \(N^{-1}\) floor is forced by
the conserved extensive energy in this ensemble, but
Theorem~\ref{thm:separated-stationary} charges stationary memory as
\(\pi_{0,S}^2\), so an \(O(N^{-1})\) zero-mode weight contributes only
\(O(N^{-2})\) to the mean-square stationary trace-distance error.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:weak-ETH-zero-new}
Under nondegenerate energies,
\begin{equation}
  \pi_{0,S}
  \le
  \frac{2d}{d^2-1}
  \delta_S(H).
  \label{eq:weak-ETH-zero-new}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_q\) be the Hermitian subsystem basis from
Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-operator-basis}, and
\(O_a=P_a\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B\).  Since the energies are nondegenerate,
\(\mathsf Q_0\) projects onto the span of
\(\{\ket n\!\bra n\}_n\).  Therefore
\[
  \left\lVert\mathsf Q_0O_a\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  =
  \frac1D
  \sum_n
  |\bra nO_a\ket n|^2.
\]
Set
\[
  X_n
  =
  \rho_S^{(n)}-\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}.
\]
Since \(P_a\) is traceless,
\[
  \bra nO_a\ket n
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}(P_aX_n).
\]
Parseval on the traceless subsystem operator space gives
\[
  \sum_{a=1}^{q}
  |\operatorname{Tr}(P_aX_n)|^2
  =
  d\,\operatorname{Tr}(X_n^2).
\]
Consequently
\begin{align}
  \pi_{0,S}
  &=
  \frac1q
  \sum_a
  \left\lVert\mathsf Q_0O_a\right\rVert_{2,D}^2
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \frac{d}{qD}
  \sum_n\operatorname{Tr}(X_n^2).
  \label{eq:pi0-Xn-new}
\end{align}
Every eigenvalue of \(X_n\) lies in
\([-1/d,1-1/d]\), so \(\left\lVertX_n\right\rVert_\infty\le1\).  Schatten H\"older gives
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(X_n^2)
  =
  \left\lVertX_n\right\rVert_2^2
  \le
  \left\lVertX_n\right\rVert_\infty\left\lVertX_n\right\rVert_1
  \le
  2D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \rho_S^{(n)},\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right).
\]
Substitute this into Eq.~\eqref{eq:pi0-Xn-new} and use
\(q=d^2-1\).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:ensemble-same-time-new}
Let \(H_N\) be random, let \(S\) be fixed, and put \(T_N=N^c\).
Suppose
\[
  \mathbb E A_S(T_N)
  \le
  N^{-2\kappa_0}.
\]
Then for every \(0<\kappa<\kappa_0\),
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb P\left[
  \widetilde\chi_S(N^{-c};H_N)>N^{-\kappa}
  \right]
  \le
  \frac{2}{c_*^2}
  N^{-2(\kappa_0-\kappa)}.
  \label{eq:ensemble-same-time-new}
\end{equation}
If in addition
\[
  \mathbb E\pi_{0,S}(H_N)\le p_N,
\]
then for every \(b_N>0\),
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb P[
  \pi_{0,S}(H_N)>b_N]
  \le
  \frac{p_N}{b_N}.
  \label{eq:pi0-Markov-new}
\end{equation}
Thus a polynomial second-moment autocorrelation theorem and independent
zero-mode control imply high-probability local equilibration on the same
windows \(T_N=N^c\).
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The first inequality of
Theorem~\ref{thm:same-scale-equivalence-new} gives
\[
  \widetilde\chi_S(N^{-c};H_N)^2
  \le
  \frac2{c_*^2}A_S(T_N).
\]
The event
\[
  \widetilde\chi_S(N^{-c};H_N)>N^{-\kappa}
\]
therefore implies
\[
  A_S(T_N)
  >
  \frac{c_*^2}{2}N^{-2\kappa}.
\]
Markov's inequality and the assumed expectation bound give
Eq.~\eqref{eq:ensemble-same-time-new}.  Equation
\eqref{eq:pi0-Markov-new} is Markov's inequality applied directly to
\(\pi_{0,S}\ge0\).  The final statement follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:separated-same-scale}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:weak-ETH-plus-mixing-new}
Let \(S\) be fixed and suppose the energies are nondegenerate.
If \(\delta_S(H_N)=O(N^{-\gamma})\) and
\(A_S(N^c)=O(N^{-2\kappa})\), then
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E_{H_N}(N^c)
 =O_S(N^{-2\gamma})+O_S(N^{-2\kappa}).
 \label{eq:weak-ETH-plus-mixing-new}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:weak-ETH-zero-new} gives
\(\pi_{0,S}=O_S(N^{-\gamma})\).
Insert this and the assumed mean-square estimate directly into
Eq.~\eqref{eq:direct-from-autocorrelation-new}.
No conversion through \(\widetilde\chi_S\) is needed.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:clock-spectrum}
For \(m=0,\ldots,n-1\), set
\[
  \theta_{m,\phi}
  =
  \frac{2\pi m}{n}-\frac{\phi}{n}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  \ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}
  =
  \frac1{\sqrt n}
  \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}
  e^{i\theta_{m,\phi}t}
  \ket{K_{t,\phi}}
  \label{eq:clock-state}
\end{equation}
is an eigenstate of \(H_{\mathrm{FK}}\) with
\begin{equation}
  E_{m,\phi}
  =
  1-\cos\theta_{m,\phi}.
  \label{eq:clock-energy}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
For \(0\le t\le n-2\),
\[
  u_tU_{t:0}=U_{t+1:0}.
\]
At the periodic boundary,
\[
  U_{n:0}\ket\phi
  =
  U_F\ket\phi
  =
  e^{i\phi}\ket\phi.
\]
Thus the Krylov basis obeys the twisted boundary condition
\[
  \ket{K_{n,\phi}}
  =
  e^{i\phi}\ket{K_{0,\phi}}.
\]
The plane-wave coefficient is consistent with this twist because
\[
  e^{i\theta_{m,\phi}n}e^{i\phi}
  =
  e^{2\pi im}
  =
  1.
\]
Acting with Eq.~\eqref{eq:FK} on
Eq.~\eqref{eq:clock-state},
\begin{align}
  H_{\mathrm{FK}}\ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}
  &=
  \left(
  1-\frac12e^{i\theta_{m,\phi}}
  -\frac12e^{-i\theta_{m,\phi}}
  \right)
  \ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}
  \nonumber\\
  &=
  \left(
  1-\cos\theta_{m,\phi}
  \right)
  \ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}.
\end{align}
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:LFSR-cycle-phases}
The classical maximal LFSR fixes the all-zero bit string and forms one
cycle of length \(L\) on the nonzero bit strings.  Consequently its
permutation unitary \(U_F\) has a two-dimensional \(+1\) eigenspace and
the remaining eigenvalues are
\begin{equation}
  e^{i\phi_q}
  =
  e^{-2\pi iq/L},
  \qquad
  q=1,\ldots,L-1.
  \label{eq:LFSR-phases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Maximality of an \(n\)-bit LFSR means precisely that its classical update
has period \(2^n-1\) on every nonzero state.  Since there are exactly
\(2^n-1\) nonzero bit strings, they form one cycle.  The zero string is
fixed by linearity.

List the nonzero cycle as
\[
  x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{L-1},
  \qquad
  U_F\ket{x_t}=\ket{x_{t+1}},
\]
with indices modulo \(L\).  The Fourier vectors
\[
  \ket{\psi_q}
  =
  \frac1{\sqrt L}
  \sum_{t=0}^{L-1}
  e^{2\pi iqt/L}\ket{x_t},
  \qquad
  q=0,\ldots,L-1,
\]
satisfy
\[
  U_F\ket{\psi_q}
  =
  e^{-2\pi iq/L}\ket{\psi_q}.
\]
The \(q=0\) vector and the fixed zero-string vector are independent
\(+1\) eigenvectors.  The cycle decomposition contains no other cycles,
so there are no further \(+1\) eigenvectors.  Removing \(q=0\) leaves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:LFSR-phases}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:LFSR-external}
For every nonidentity spin Pauli operator \(P\), and every pair of
nontrivial Floquet eigenstates \(\ket{\psi_q},\ket{\psi_{q'}}\),
\begin{equation}
  \left\lvert\bra{\psi_q}P\ket{\psi_{q'}}\right\rvert
  \le
  c_n,
  \qquad
  c_n
  :=
  \frac{2^{1+n/2}}{2^n-1}.
  \label{eq:LFSR-Pauli-input}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:LFSR-external} is an external literature input.  The
Floquet phase grid and exceptional multiplicity were proved above, and
all static spectral consequences needed below are derived explicitly.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:LFSR-static-matrix}
Let \(P\ne\mathbbm{1}\) be a spin Pauli operator, extended trivially to the clock.
For regular static eigenstates,
\begin{equation}
  \left\lvert
  \bra{\Psi_{m,q}}
  P\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{\rm clock}
  \ket{\Psi_{m',q'}}
  \right\rvert
  \le
  c_n.
  \label{eq:LFSR-static-matrix}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Using Eq.~\eqref{eq:clock-state} and clock orthogonality,
\begin{align}
  &\bra{\Psi_{m,q}}
  P\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{\rm clock}
  \ket{\Psi_{m',q'}}
  \nonumber\\
  &\qquad=
  \frac1n
  \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}
  e^{i(\theta_{m',q'}-\theta_{m,q})t}
  \bra{\psi_q}
  U_{t:0}^\dagger P U_{t:0}
  \ket{\psi_{q'}}.
\end{align}
The LFSR gates are Clifford, so
\(U_{t:0}^\dagger P U_{t:0}\)
is again a nonidentity Pauli operator.  Apply
Eq.~\eqref{eq:LFSR-Pauli-input} term by term and use the triangle
inequality.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:arcsine}
The measure \(\nu\) is supported on \([0,2]\) and has density
\begin{equation}
  f_E(u)
  =
  \frac{
  \mathbbm 1_{(0,2)}(u)
  }{
  \pi\sqrt{u(2-u)}
  }.
  \label{eq:energy-density}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Let
\[
  X=\cos\Theta.
\]
For \(x\in(-1,1)\), the equation \(\cos\theta=x\) has two solutions in
\([0,2\pi)\), and on each branch
\[
  \left|\frac{d\theta}{dx}\right|
  =
  \frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}.
\]
Since \(\Theta\) has density \(1/(2\pi)\), summing the two branches gives
\[
  f_X(x)
  =
  \frac1{\pi\sqrt{1-x^2}},
  \qquad -1<x<1.
\]
Now \(E=1-X\).  Therefore
\[
  f_E(u)
  =
  f_X(1-u)
  =
  \frac1{
  \pi\sqrt{1-(1-u)^2}
  }
  =
  \frac1{
  \pi\sqrt{u(2-u)}
  },
\]
for \(0<u<2\).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:grid-interval}
Let \(\Theta_M=\{2\pi a/M:a=0,\ldots,M-1\}\).
For every interval \(J\subset[0,2\pi)\), with any included or excluded
finite endpoints,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\#(\Theta_M\cap J)-\frac{M|J|}{2\pi}\right|\le1.
 \label{eq:grid-interval}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Rescale the endpoints by \(M/(2\pi)\).
For an interval with endpoints \(a\le b\), the integer counts for
\([a,b]\), \([a,b)\), \((a,b]\), and \((a,b)\) are, respectively,
\[
 \max(0,\lfloor b\rfloor-\lceil a\rceil+1),\quad
 \max(0,\lceil b\rceil-\lceil a\rceil),\quad
 \max(0,\lfloor b\rfloor-\lfloor a\rfloor),\quad
 \max(0,\lceil b\rceil-\lfloor a\rfloor-1).
\]
The inequalities \(x-1<\lfloor x\rfloor\le x\) and
\(x\le\lceil x\rceil<x+1\), including the equality cases at integers,
show that each count differs from \(b-a\) by at most one.
The empty-interval and singleton cases obey the same bound.
Since \(J\subset[0,2\pi)\), rescaling includes no grid integers outside
\(0,\ldots,M-1\).  This proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:kolmogorov}
Let
\[
  F_M(y)=\nu_M((-\infty,y]),
  \qquad
  F(y)=\nu((-\infty,y]).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{y\in\mathbb R}
  |F_M(y)-F(y)|
  \le
  \frac2M.
  \label{eq:kolmogorov}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
For \(y<0\) or \(y\ge2\), the claim is immediate.  Let \(0\le y<2\) and
define
\[
  \alpha=\arccos(1-y)\in[0,\pi).
\]
The condition
\[
  1-\cos\theta\le y
\]
is equivalent to
\[
  \theta\in[0,\alpha]\cup[2\pi-\alpha,2\pi).
\]
The two intervals are disjoint and have total length \(2\alpha\).
At \(\alpha=0\) the first is a singleton and the second is empty.
Lemma~\ref{lem:grid-interval} bounds each interval's counting error in
absolute value by one, so their union has counting error at most two.  Dividing by \(M\) gives
\[
  |F_M(y)-\alpha/\pi|
  \le\frac2M.
\]
Since \(\alpha/\pi=F(y)\), the result follows.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:BV}
Let \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) be probability measures with distribution functions
\(G_1,G_2\), and suppose
\(\sup_y|G_1(y)-G_2(y)|\le\eta\).
If \(h\) is absolutely continuous, has compact support, and
\(h'\in L^1(\mathbb R)\), then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\int h\,d\mu_1-\int h\,d\mu_2\right|
 \le\eta\int_{\mathbb R}|h'(y)|dy.
 \label{eq:BV}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Put \(\sigma=\mu_1-\mu_2\).  Since \(h\) has compact support and is
absolutely continuous,
\(h(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x h'(y)dy\).
Absolute integrability with respect to \(|\sigma|\) and Lebesgue
measure follows from
\(|\sigma|(\mathbb R)\int|h'|\le2\int|h'|<\infty\).
Interchanging integrals consequently gives
\[
 \int h\,d\sigma
 =\int h'(y)\sigma([y,\infty))dy
 =-\int h'(y)\sigma((-\infty,y))dy.
\]
The two distribution functions have left limits, whose difference is
also bounded by \(\eta\).  Taking absolute values proves the claim.
The absolute-continuity hypothesis is sufficient for all uses below;
it avoids any convention about simultaneous Stieltjes jumps.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:difference-density}
The random variable \(Z\) has an even density \(g\) supported on
\([-2,2]\).  For \(0<z<2\),
\begin{equation}
  g(z)
  =
  \frac1{\pi^2}
  \int_{z-1}^{1}
  \frac{dx}{
  \sqrt{
  (1-x^2)
  (1-(x-z)^2)
  }
  }.
  \label{eq:g-convolution}
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
  g(z)
  \le
  \log\left(\frac4{|z|}\right),
  \qquad
  0<|z|<2.
  \label{eq:g-log}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The convolution formula gives
\[
  g(z)
  =
  \int_{\mathbb R}f(x)f(x-z)\,dx.
\]
For \(0<z<2\), both factors are nonzero precisely when
\[
  x\in[z-1,1],
\]
which proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:g-convolution}.  Since \(X-Y\) and \(Y-X\)
have the same distribution, \(g\) is even.

Fix \(0<z<2\), put
\[
  L=2-z,
\]
and make the change of variables
\[
  x=z-1+Lt,
  \qquad 0\le t\le1.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
  1-x&=L(1-t),\\
  1+x&=z+Lt,\\
  1-x+z&=2-Lt,\\
  1+x-z&=Lt.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  g(z)
  =
  \frac1{\pi^2}
  \int_0^1
  \frac{dt}{
  \sqrt{
  t(1-t)(z+Lt)(2-Lt)
  }
  }.
  \label{eq:g-t}
\end{equation}

First assume \(0<z\le1\), so \(L\ge1\).  On \(0<t\le1/2\),
\[
  1-t\ge\frac12,
  \qquad
  2-Lt
  \ge
  2-\frac L2
  =
  1+\frac z2
  \ge1,
\]
and
\[
  z+Lt\ge z+t.
\]
Thus the integrand in Eq.~\eqref{eq:g-t} is at most
\[
  \frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt{t(z+t)}}.
\]
The integrand in Eq.~\eqref{eq:g-t} is invariant under
\(t\mapsto1-t\), because this transformation exchanges
\(z+Lt\) and \(2-Lt\).  Hence
\begin{align*}
  g(z)
  &\le
  \frac{2\sqrt2}{\pi^2}
  \int_0^{1/2}
  \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t(z+t)}}.
\end{align*}
With \(t=z\sinh^2u\),
\[
  \int_0^a
  \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t(z+t)}}
  =
  2\,\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt{\frac az}.
\]
Therefore
\[
  g(z)
  \le
  \frac{4\sqrt2}{\pi^2}
  \operatorname{arsinh}
  \frac1{\sqrt{2z}}.
\]
Using
\[
  \operatorname{arsinh}y
  =
  \log(y+\sqrt{1+y^2})
  \le
  \log(1+2y)
\]
for \(y\ge0\), and
\[
  1+\sqrt{\frac2z}
  \le
  \frac4z
  \qquad (0<z\le1),
\]
we obtain
\[
  g(z)
  \le
  \frac{4\sqrt2}{\pi^2}
  \log\frac4z
  \le
  \log\frac4z,
\]
because \(4\sqrt2/\pi^2<1\).

Now assume \(1\le z<2\), so \(0<L\le1\).  For every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
  z+Lt\ge1,
  \qquad
  2-Lt\ge2-L=z\ge1.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:g-t} gives
\[
  g(z)
  \le
  \frac1{\pi^2}
  \int_0^1\frac{dt}{\sqrt{t(1-t)}}
  =
  \frac1\pi.
\]
Since
\[
  \log\frac4z\ge\log2>\frac1\pi
\]
for \(1\le z<2\), Eq.~\eqref{eq:g-log} follows in this case as well.
Evenness gives the negative-\(z\) half.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:continuum-concentration}
For every interval \(I\subset\mathbb R\) of length
\(0<\delta\le1\),
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb P(Z\in I)
  \le
  2\delta
  \log\left(\frac{4e}{\delta}\right).
  \label{eq:continuum-concentration}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:difference-density},
\[
  g(z)\le\log\frac4{|z|}
\]
on the support \([-2,2]\), away from \(z=0\).  Use the
nonnegative envelope
\(h(z)=\mathbbm1_{\{0<|z|\le2\}}\log(4/|z|)\), with its value
at zero immaterial for integration.  It is even and nonincreasing
on the positive half-line.  The positive and negative parts of an
interval of length \(\delta\) each have length at most \(\delta\).
Their integrals are therefore each bounded by
\(\int_0^\delta h(z)\,dz\).  Consequently
\[
  \mathbb P(Z\in I)\le\int_I h(z)\,dz
  \le 2\int_0^\delta\log\frac4z\,dz.
\]
The integral is explicit:
\[
  \int_0^\delta\log\frac4z\,dz
  =
  \delta\log\frac4\delta+\delta
  =
  \delta\log\frac{4e}{\delta}.
\]
This proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:continuum-concentration}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:cosine-difference-discrepancy}
Let \(U,V\) be independent with law \(\nu_M\), and \(E_1,E_2\)
independent with the continuous law \(\nu\).
For every \(I=[a,b)\), \(a<b\),
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathbb P(U-V\in I)-\mathbb P(E_1-E_2\in I)\right|
 \le\frac8M.
 \label{eq:two-sided-difference-discrepancy}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
For fixed \(u\), the event \(u-V\in[a,b)\) is
\(V\in(u-b,u-a]\).  Its probability is
\[
 h_M(u)=F_M(u-a)-F_M(u-b).
\]
For the continuous law it is
\(h(u)=F(u-a)-F(u-b)\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:kolmogorov} gives
\(|h_M(u)-h(u)|\le4/M\).
The function \(h\) has compact support, is absolutely continuous, and
has derivative \(f_E(u-a)-f_E(u-b)\) almost everywhere.
Since \(\int f_E=1\), its derivative has \(L^1\) norm at most two.
Lemma~\ref{lem:BV} therefore gives
\[
 \left|\int h_M\,d\nu_M-\int h\,d\nu\right|
 \le\int|h_M-h|\,d\nu_M
       +\left|\int h\,d(\nu_M-\nu)\right|
 \le\frac4M+\frac2M\,2=\frac8M.
\]
These two integrals are the difference probabilities in question.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:cosine-difference}
For every integer \(M\ge1\) and \(0<\delta\le1\),
\begin{equation}
 N_M(\delta)\le
 2M^2\delta\log(4e/\delta)+8M.
 \label{eq:cosine-difference}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
For \(I=[x,x+\delta)\), its normalized ordered-pair count is
\(\mathbb P(U-V\in I)\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:cosine-difference-discrepancy} bounds this by the
continuous difference probability plus \(8/M\).
Since \(E_1-E_2\) is a difference of two arcsine variables,
Lemma~\ref{lem:continuum-concentration} bounds that probability by
\(2\delta\log(4e/\delta)\).
Multiply by \(M^2\) and take the supremum over \(x\).
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
Counting one energy at a time gives \(O(M^2\sqrt\delta)\).  Theorem
\ref{thm:cosine-difference} replaces the square root by
\(\delta\log(1/\delta)\).  The logarithm is natural: it is the singularity
of the difference density at zero.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:improved-chi}
Under Theorem~\ref{thm:LFSR-external} and Lemma~\ref{lem:LFSR-static-matrix}, for every \(0<\delta\le1\),
\begin{equation}
  \chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm FK})
  \le
  8n\delta
  \log\left(\frac{4e}{\delta}\right)
  +
  \frac{32}{2^n-1}
  +
  \frac4{2^n}.
  \label{eq:improved-chi}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
  \chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm FK})
  =
  O\!\left(
  n\delta\log\frac e\delta
  \right)
  +
  O(2^{-n}).
  \label{eq:improved-chi-O}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Let \(I\) be a frequency interval of width \(\delta\).
The regular energies form a subset of the full \(M\)-point cosine grid.
Therefore the number \(N_{\mathcal R}(I)\) of ordered regular pairs
\((j,k)\) with \(E_j-E_k\in I\) is no larger than the full-grid count of
Theorem~\ref{thm:cosine-difference}:
\begin{equation}
  N_{\mathcal R}(I)
  \le
  2M^2\delta
  \log\left(\frac{4e}{\delta}\right)
  +
  8M.
  \label{eq:NR-improved}
\end{equation}

For regular pairs, Lemma~\ref{lem:LFSR-static-matrix} gives
\[
  |\bra jO_a\ket k|^2\le c_n^2.
\]
Hence their contribution to
Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-weight-matrix} is at most
\[
  \frac{N_{\mathcal R}(I)c_n^2}{D}.
\]

Now consider pairs for which at least one index is exceptional.  Since
\(O_a\) is unitary,
\[
  \sum_k|\bra jO_a\ket k|^2
  =
  \bra jO_a^\dagger O_a\ket j
  =
  1.
\]
There are \(r=2n\) exceptional choices of \(j\), so all pairs with
exceptional first index contribute at most \(r/D\).  The same argument
with the second index contributes at most another \(r/D\).  Counting their
intersection twice only increases the upper bound.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
  \langle O_a,\mathsf Q_IO_a\rangle
  \le
  \frac{N_{\mathcal R}(I)c_n^2}{D}
  +
  \frac{2r}{D}.
  \label{eq:weight-before-algebra}
\end{equation}

We now evaluate the coefficients exactly.  Recall
\[
  M=n(2^n-1),
  \qquad
  D=n2^n,
  \qquad
  c_n^2
  =
  \frac{2^{n+2}}{(2^n-1)^2}.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
  \frac{M^2c_n^2}{D}
  &=
  \frac{
  n^2(2^n-1)^2
  }{
  n2^n
  }
  \frac{
  2^{n+2}
  }{
  (2^n-1)^2
  }
  =
  4n,
  \label{eq:M2-exact}\\
  \frac{8Mc_n^2}{D}
  &=
  8
  \frac{
  n(2^n-1)
  }{
  n2^n
  }
  \frac{
  2^{n+2}
  }{
  (2^n-1)^2
  }
  =
  \frac{32}{2^n-1},
  \label{eq:M-exact}\\
  \frac{2r}{D}
  &=
  \frac{4n}{n2^n}
  =
  \frac4{2^n}.
  \label{eq:r-exact}
\end{align}
Substituting Eq.~\eqref{eq:NR-improved} into
Eq.~\eqref{eq:weight-before-algebra} and then using
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:M2-exact}--\eqref{eq:r-exact} gives
\[
  \langle O_a,\mathsf Q_IO_a\rangle
  \le
  8n\delta
  \log\left(\frac{4e}{\delta}\right)
  +
  \frac{32}{2^n-1}
  +
  \frac4{2^n}.
\]
The right-hand side is independent of \(a\).  Averaging over the
\(q\) local Pauli strings and taking the supremum over \(I\) proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:improved-chi}.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:zero}
Let
\[
  \pi_{0,S}
  =
  \mu_S(\{0\}).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  \pi_{0,S}
  \le
  \frac{32}{2^n-1}
  +
  \frac4{2^n}
  =
  O(2^{-n}).
  \label{eq:zero}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
For every \(\delta>0\), the interval \([0,\delta)\) contains the zero
frequency, hence
\[
  \pi_{0,S}\le\chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm FK}).
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:improved-chi} and take
\(\delta\downarrow0\).  Since
\[
  \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
  \delta\log\frac{4e}{\delta}
  =0,
\]
the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:LFSR-infinite-improved}
For every fixed spin-only subsystem \(S\),
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{\rho_S}
  \overline{
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{2^s}
  \right)^2
  }
  =
  O_s(2^{-n}).
  \label{eq:LFSR-infinite-improved}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
For fixed \(0<\delta\le1\), take \(T\to\infty\) in
Theorem~\ref{thm:fejer-local-band}.  Since
\[
  \lim_{T\to\infty}
  \left[
  1+\frac{2\pi^2}{3(T\delta)^2}
  \right]
  =1,
\]
we obtain
\[
  \sup_{\rho_S}
  \overline{
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2
  }
  \le
  (d-1)q^2\chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm FK}).
\]
Now take \(\delta\downarrow0\) and use
Theorem~\ref{thm:improved-chi}.  Its first term tends to zero and the
remaining terms are \(O(2^{-n})\).  Since \(d=2^s\) is fixed, the
prefactor is independent of \(n\).
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:LFSR-stationary-improved}
For the temporal channel
\(\overline{\Phi}\),
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{\rho_S}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{2^s}
  \right)
  =
  O_s(2^{-n}).
  \label{eq:LFSR-stationary-improved}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:separated-stationary} gives
\[
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \overline{\Phi}(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)
  \le
  \frac{\sqrt{d-1}}2\,q\,\pi_{0,S}.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:zero} gives
\(\pi_{0,S}=O(2^{-n})\).
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:LFSR-direct-T}
For every fixed spin-only subsystem \(S\), there exists
\(C_s>0\) such that for every \(n\) and every \(T\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t_0\ge0}\sup_{\rho_S}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{2^s}
  \right)^2dt
  \le
  C_s
  \left[
  \frac{n\log(eT)}{T}
  +
  2^{-n}
  \right].
  \label{eq:LFSR-direct-T}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Set \(\varepsilon=T^{-1}\) in
Theorem~\ref{thm:fejer-local-band}.  Since \(T\ge1\),
\(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and Theorem~\ref{thm:improved-chi} gives
\[
  \chi_S(T^{-1};H_{\rm FK})
  \le
  \frac{8n}{T}\log(4eT)
  +
  \frac{32}{2^n-1}
  +
  \frac4{2^n}.
\]
Furthermore
\[
  \log(4eT)
  \le
  (1+\log4)\log(eT)
\]
because \(\log(eT)\ge1\).  For \(n\ge2\),
\[
  \frac{32}{2^n-1}+\frac4{2^n}
  \le47\,2^{-n}.
\]
The finitely many smaller values of \(n\) can be absorbed into the same
constant \(C_s\).  Equation~\eqref{eq:fejer-local-trace} with
\(T\varepsilon=1\) completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:LFSR-alpha-improved}
For every fixed \(\alpha>0\),
\begin{equation}
  T_n
  =
  n^{1+\alpha}\log(en)
  \label{eq:LFSR-T-alpha}
\end{equation}
implies
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t_0,\rho_S}
  \frac1{T_n}
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T_n}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{2^s}
  \right)^2dt
  =
  O_{s,\alpha}(n^{-\alpha})
  +
  O_s(2^{-n}).
  \label{eq:LFSR-alpha-improved}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
  T_n=n^2\log(en)
  \label{eq:LFSR-n2log}
\end{equation}
is sufficient for mean-square error \(O_s(n^{-1})\).
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{eq:LFSR-T-alpha} gives
\[
  \log(eT_n)
  =
  1+(1+\alpha)\log n+\log\log(en)
  =
  O_\alpha(\log(en)).
\]
Therefore
\[
  \frac{n\log(eT_n)}{T_n}
  =
  O_\alpha(n^{-\alpha}).
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:LFSR-direct-T}.  Setting \(\alpha=1\) gives
Eq.~\eqref{eq:LFSR-n2log}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:LFSR-small-gap-improved}
The smallest positive energy in the one-clock-particle sector obeys
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_n
  \le
  1-
  \cos\left(
  \frac{2\pi}{n(2^n-1)}
  \right)
  \le
  \frac{2\pi^2}{
  n^2(2^n-1)^2
  }
  =
  O(n^{-2}4^{-n}).
  \label{eq:LFSR-small-gap-improved}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\[
  \Delta_n^{-1}
  =
  \Omega(n^24^n).
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Choose \(m=0\) and \(q=1\) in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:LFSR-energy}.  This gives a positive energy
\[
  1-
  \cos\left(
  \frac{2\pi}{n(2^n-1)}
  \right).
\]
The smallest positive energy is no larger than this value.  Finally use
\[
  1-\cos x\le\frac{x^2}{2}.
\]
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:difference-lower}
Let \(g\) be the density in
Lemma~\ref{lem:difference-density}.  For every \(0<z\le1/2\),
\begin{equation}
  g(z)
  \ge
  \frac1{2\sqrt2\,\pi^2}
  \log\frac1z.
  \label{eq:g-lower}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Starting from Eq.~\eqref{eq:g-convolution}, substitute
\[
  y=1-x.
\]
Then
\[
  1-x^2=y(2-y),
\]
and
\[
  1-(x-z)^2
  =
  (y+z)(2-y-z).
\]
For \(0<z\le1/2\), restrict the integral to
\[
  z\le y\le1.
\]
On this interval,
\[
  2-y\le2,
  \qquad
  2-y-z\le2.
\]
Therefore
\[
  \sqrt{
  (1-x^2)(1-(x-z)^2)
  }
  \le
  2\sqrt{y(y+z)}.
\]
Also, because \(y\ge z\),
\[
  y+z\le2y,
\]
hence
\[
  \sqrt{y(y+z)}
  \le
  \sqrt2\,y.
\]
Thus
\[
  g(z)
  \ge
  \frac1{\pi^2}
  \int_z^1
  \frac{dy}{2\sqrt2\,y}
  =
  \frac1{2\sqrt2\,\pi^2}
  \log\frac1z.
\]
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:theta-log}
There exist absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that for every
\(0<\delta\le1/2\),
\begin{equation}
  c\,\delta\log\frac1\delta
  \le
  \mathbb P(0\le Z\le\delta)
  \le
  C\,\delta\log\frac e\delta.
  \label{eq:theta-log}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
The upper bound is
Lemma~\ref{lem:continuum-concentration}.  For the lower bound, integrate
Eq.~\eqref{eq:g-lower}:
\begin{align*}
  \mathbb P(0\le Z\le\delta)
  &\ge
  \frac1{2\sqrt2\,\pi^2}
  \int_0^\delta\log\frac1z\,dz\\
  &=
  \frac1{2\sqrt2\,\pi^2}
  \left[
  \delta\log\frac1\delta+\delta
  \right]\\
  &\ge
  \frac1{2\sqrt2\,\pi^2}
  \delta\log\frac1\delta.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:discrete-lower}
Let \(N_M(\delta)\) be defined by Eq.~\eqref{eq:NM}.  There is an absolute
constant \(c>0\) such that, for \(0<\delta\le1/2\),
\begin{equation}
  N_M(\delta)
  \ge
  cM^2\delta\log\frac1\delta
  -
  8M.
  \label{eq:discrete-lower}
\end{equation}
In particular, if
\[
  M\delta\log(1/\delta)\longrightarrow\infty,
\]
then
\[
  N_M(\delta)
  =
  \Theta\left(
  M^2\delta\log\frac1\delta
  \right)
\]
up to absolute constants.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Use \(I=[0,\delta)\) in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cosine-difference-discrepancy}.  The continuous difference
law has no atoms, so Corollary~\ref{cor:theta-log} gives
\(\mathbb P(E_1-E_2\in I)\ge
 c\delta\log(1/\delta)\).
Hence its discrete counterpart is at least this quantity minus \(8/M\).
Multiplication by \(M^2\) proves the asserted lower bound for the
half-open interval \(I\), which is one of the intervals in the
definition of \(N_M\).
If \(M\delta\log(1/\delta)\to\infty\), the \(8M\) error is smaller than
half this leading lower bound for all sufficiently large sizes.
The upper bound from Theorem~\ref{thm:cosine-difference} has the same
order: on \(0<\delta\le1/2\),
\(\log(4e/\delta)\le
[1+\log(4e)/\log2]\log(1/\delta)\).
This proves the two-sided asymptotic assertion.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:last-log}
Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-lower} prevents replacing the unweighted
cosine-difference count by \(O(M^2\delta)\) throughout the stated
regime.  It does \emph{not} prove a matching
\(\log T/T\) lower bound on subsystem relaxation.
A direct weighted collision estimate, finer matrix-element information,
or another dynamical argument might improve the clock rate without
improving the maximum unweighted interval count.
The strongest clock rate established in these notes remains
Eq.~\eqref{eq:LFSR-direct-T}; no \(O_s(n/T)\) clock theorem is claimed.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:general-clock-matrix}
For every normalized traceless local unitary basis element \(O_a\) on the
fixed spin subsystem and every pair \(j,k\) of regular static-clock
eigenstates,
\begin{equation}
  |\bra jO_a\ket k|
  \le c_Q.
  \label{eq:general-clock-cQ}
\end{equation}
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:general-clock}
Under the distinct-phase grid hypothesis above and
Assumption~\ref{ass:general-clock-matrix}, for every \(0<\delta\le1\),
\begin{equation}
  \chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm clock})
  \le
  \frac{2KL^2c_Q^2}{Q}
  \delta\log\frac{4e}{\delta}
  +
  \frac{8Lc_Q^2}{Q}
  +
  \frac{2r_F}{Q}.
\label{eq:general-clock-chi}
\end{equation}
In particular, if
\[
  c_Q\le\frac{C}{\sqrt Q},
  \qquad
  L\le Q,
  \qquad
  r_F\le r_0
\]
with constants \(C,r_0\) independent of \(Q,K\), then
\begin{equation}
  \chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm clock})
  \le
  2C^2K\delta\log\frac{4e}{\delta}
  +
  \frac{8C^2+2r_0}{Q}.
  \label{eq:general-clock-simple}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
If a regular Floquet vector has phase label \(q\), its clock
branches have lifted labels \(mL+q\), \(0\le m<K\).
Distinct regular vectors have distinct \(q\), so the map from regular
static states to these \(M=KL\) labels is injective.  Equal cosine
energies can still occur; they are already counted with their distinct
grid labels in Theorem~\ref{thm:cosine-difference}.  Hence
Theorem~\ref{thm:cosine-difference} gives, for every frequency interval
\(I\) of width \(\delta\),
\[
  N_{\mathcal R}(I)
  \le
  2K^2L^2\delta\log\frac{4e}{\delta}
  +
  8KL.
\]
For a normalized local unitary \(O_a\), the regular-pair contribution to
the local spectral weight is at most
\[
  \frac{N_{\mathcal R}(I)c_Q^2}{D}
  =
  \frac{N_{\mathcal R}(I)c_Q^2}{KQ}.
\]
There are at most \(Kr_F\) exceptional static eigenstates.  Unitarity of
\(O_a\) gives
\[
  \sum_k|\bra jO_a\ket k|^2=1.
\]
Therefore pairs with an exceptional first index contribute at most
\[
  \frac{Kr_F}{D}
  =
  \frac{r_F}{Q},
\]
and the same bound holds for exceptional second index.  Adding the three
contributions gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:general-clock-chi}.

If \(c_Q^2\le C^2/Q\) and \(L\le Q\), then
\[
  \frac{L^2c_Q^2}{Q}
  \le C^2,
  \qquad
  \frac{Lc_Q^2}{Q}
  \le\frac{C^2}{Q}.
\]
Substitution proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:general-clock-simple}.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:general-clock-window}
Under the simplified hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:general-clock}, for every fixed subsystem \(S\) there is
a constant \(C_S\) such that, for every \(T\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t_0,\rho_S}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2dt
  \le
  C_S
  \left[
  \frac{K\log(eT)}{T}
  +
  \frac1Q
  \right].
  \label{eq:general-clock-window}
\end{equation}
For every fixed \(\alpha>0\), if \(Q\) grows exponentially in \(K\),
target mean-square error \(O(K^{-\alpha})\) is therefore reached on
\[
  T_K=O_\alpha(K^{1+\alpha}\log K).
\]
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Set \(\delta=T^{-1}\) in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:general-clock-simple} and apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:fejer-local-band}.  Since
\(T\delta=1\), the Fej\'er prefactor is an absolute constant, and all
remaining subsystem factors are fixed.  This proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:general-clock-window}.  If
\(T_K=K^{1+\alpha}\log(eK)\), then
\[
  \log(eT_K)=O_\alpha(\log(eK))
\]
and therefore
\[
  \frac{K\log(eT_K)}{T_K}
  =
  O_\alpha(K^{-\alpha}).
\]
If \(Q\) grows exponentially in \(K\), the term \(Q^{-1}\) is smaller
than every inverse power of \(K\), completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:companion-staircase}
On the computational basis
\(\ket{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}}\), define the two-site permutation gates
\begin{equation}
  g_i\ket{a,b}
  =
  \ket{b,a-f_i b},
  \qquad
  1\le i\le n-1,
  \label{eq:gi-prime-power}
\end{equation}
where \(g_i\) acts on sites \(i-1,i\), and define the one-site gate
\begin{equation}
  g_0\ket a
  =
  \ket{-f_0a}
  \label{eq:g0-prime-power}
\end{equation}
on site \(0\).  Then
\begin{equation}
  U_F
  :=
  g_0g_1\cdots g_{n-1},
  \label{eq:UF-staircase}
\end{equation}
with \(g_{n-1}\) applied first, implements the companion map
\begin{align}
  F(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})
  &=
  \bigl(
  -f_0x_{n-1},
  x_0-f_1x_{n-1},
  \ldots,
  x_{n-2}-f_{n-1}x_{n-1}
  \bigr).
  \label{eq:companion-map}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
We prove by descending induction on \(k\) the effect of applying
\[
  g_k g_{k+1}\cdots g_{n-1}
\]
with \(g_{n-1}\) first.  After these gates, the entries on sites
\(0,\ldots,k-2\) are still
\[
  x_0,\ldots,x_{k-2},
\]
site \(k-1\) contains \(x_{n-1}\), and sites
\(j=k,\ldots,n-1\) contain
\[
  x_{j-1}-f_jx_{n-1}.
\]
For \(k=n-1\), this follows directly from
Eq.~\eqref{eq:gi-prime-power}.  Assume it holds for \(k\ge2\).
Gate \(g_{k-1}\) acts on sites \(k-2,k-1\), whose entries before that gate
are \(x_{k-2}\) and \(x_{n-1}\).  It maps them to
\[
  x_{n-1},
  \qquad
  x_{k-2}-f_{k-1}x_{n-1},
\]
and leaves all other entries unchanged.  This is exactly the induction
statement with \(k\) replaced by \(k-1\).

After the final two-site gate \(g_1\), the register therefore equals
\[
  \bigl(
  x_{n-1},
  x_0-f_1x_{n-1},
  \ldots,
  x_{n-2}-f_{n-1}x_{n-1}
  \bigr).
\]
Applying \(g_0\) to the first site gives
Eq.~\eqref{eq:companion-map}.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:prime-power-cycle}
The map \(F\) fixes the zero vector and acts as one cycle of length
\(L=Q-1\) on
\(\mathbb F_{q_0}^n\setminus\{0\}\).  Consequently the permutation
unitary \(U_F\) has a two-dimensional \(+1\) eigenspace.  Its remaining
Floquet eigenphases may be labelled as
\begin{equation}
  \phi_q
  =
  -\frac{2\pi q}{L},
  \qquad
  q=1,\ldots,L-1.
  \label{eq:prime-power-phases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Let \(\alpha\) be a root of the primitive polynomial \(f\).  The vector
space \(\mathbb F_{q_0}^n\) is canonically identified with
\(\mathbb F_{q_0^n}\) in the basis
\[
  1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{n-1}.
\]
The companion map is multiplication by \(\alpha\).  Because \(f\) is
primitive, \(\alpha\) generates the multiplicative group
\[
  \mathbb F_{q_0^n}^{\times},
\]
which has order \(Q-1=L\).  Thus \(0\) is fixed and all nonzero vectors
form one orbit of length \(L\).

Let \(\ket{x_t}\), \(t\in\mathbb Z_L\), list that orbit so that
\(U_F\ket{x_t}=\ket{x_{t+1}}\).  The Fourier vectors
\[
  \ket{\psi_q}
  =
  \frac1{\sqrt L}
  \sum_{t=0}^{L-1}
  e^{2\pi iqt/L}\ket{x_t},
  \qquad
  q=0,\ldots,L-1,
\]
satisfy
\[
  U_F\ket{\psi_q}
  =
  e^{-2\pi iq/L}\ket{\psi_q}.
\]
The \(q=0\) Fourier vector and the fixed vector \(\ket0\) are linearly
independent \(+1\) eigenvectors, and there are no others because the
cycle decomposition has exactly two cycles.  This proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:character-trace-pairing}
Let \(q_0=p^r\), \(Q=q_0^n\), and let
\(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}\) be an \(\mathbb F_{q_0}\)-basis of
\(\mathbb F_Q\).  There is a unique dual basis \(b_i^\vee\) satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_{q_0}}(b_i^\vee b_k)
 =\delta_{ik}.
\]
For \(x=\sum_k x_kb_k\) and \(\beta_w=\sum_iw_i b_i^\vee\),
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_p}(\beta_wx)
 =\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_{q_0}/\mathbb F_p}
     \left(\sum_iw_ix_i\right).
\]
If \(w\ne0\), the resulting additive character of \(\mathbb F_Q\)
\[
 \psi_w(x)=\exp\!\left[
  \frac{2\pi i}{p}\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_p}(\beta_wx)
 \right]
\]
is nontrivial.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Write
\[
 T(x)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_{q_0}}(x)
     =\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}x^{q_0^k}.
\]
The identities \((x+y)^{q_0^k}=x^{q_0^k}+y^{q_0^k}\) and
\(a^{q_0^k}=a\) for \(a\in\mathbb F_{q_0}\) show that \(T\) is
\(\mathbb F_{q_0}\)-linear.  Also \(T(x)^{q_0}=T(x)\), because
\(x^{q_0^n}=x\), so its values belong to \(\mathbb F_{q_0}\).
The polynomial \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}X^{q_0^k}\) is nonzero and has degree
