\(q_0^{n-1}<Q\).  A nonzero polynomial of degree \(d\) over a field has
at most \(d\) roots: each root gives a linear factor, and successive
factorization reduces the degree.  Thus \(T\) is not identically zero.
Choose \(y\) with \(T(y)\ne0\).  For any \(z\ne0\), the choice
\(x=y/z\) gives \(T(zx)=T(y)\ne0\).  The bilinear pairing
\((z,x)\mapsto T(zx)\) is therefore nondegenerate.  Its Gram matrix in
any basis is invertible, which gives existence and uniqueness of the
dual basis by solving the associated linear system.

Relative and absolute traces satisfy transitivity.  Explicitly,
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_{q_0}/\mathbb F_p}(T(z))
 =\sum_{a=0}^{r-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}z^{p^{a+rk}}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{rn-1}z^{p^j}
 =\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_p}(z).
\]
Applying this identity to \(z=\beta_wx\), the defining property of the
dual basis gives \(T(\beta_wx)=\sum_iw_ix_i\), proving the stated
formula.  The same polynomial argument applied to the absolute trace
shows that it is a nonzero \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear map into
\(\mathbb F_p\), hence surjective.  If \(w\ne0\), then
\(\beta_w\ne0\).  Choose \(z\) of absolute trace one and set
\(x=z/\beta_w\).  Then \(\psi_w(x)=e^{2\pi i/p}\ne1\), proving
nontriviality.  None of these steps requires \(p\nmid n\).
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:elementary-gauss-jacobi}
Let \(\mathbb F_Q\) be a finite field and \(\psi\) a nontrivial
additive character.  Extend every multiplicative character by zero at
zero.  Define
\[
 G(A)=\sum_{x\ne0}A(x)\psi(x),\qquad
 J(A,B)=\sum_{x\ne0,1}A(x)B(1-x).
\]
If \(A\) is nontrivial, \(|G(A)|=\sqrt Q\); if \(A=1\) on
\(\mathbb F_Q^\times\), then \(G(A)=-1\).
If \(A,B\) are nontrivial, then
\[
 |J(A,B)|=\sqrt Q\quad\hbox{when }AB\ne1,
 \qquad
 J(A,A^{-1})=-A(-1).
\]
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
A nontrivial character sums to zero over its finite group.  Indeed,
choose a group element on which it is not one; translation (for an
additive group) or multiplication (for a multiplicative group) preserves
the sum but multiplies it by a character value different from one.  The sum must
therefore vanish.  Hence
\(\sum_x\psi(x)=0\) and, for nontrivial \(A\),
\(\sum_{u\ne0}A(u)=0\).
For nontrivial \(A\), substitute \(x=uy\) in the squared Gauss sum:
\begin{align*}
 |G(A)|^2
 &=\sum_{x,y\ne0}A(x)\overline{A(y)}\psi(x-y)\\
 &=\sum_{u\ne0}A(u)\sum_{y\ne0}\psi((u-1)y)\\
 &=(Q-1)-\sum_{u\ne0,1}A(u)=Q.
\end{align*}
The inner sum is \(Q-1\) for \(u=1\) and \(-1\) otherwise, since
multiplication by \(u-1\ne0\) permutes \(\mathbb F_Q^\times\).
For the trivial multiplicative character, the Gauss sum is directly
\(\sum_{x\ne0}\psi(x)=-1\).

Suppose \(A,B,AB\) are nontrivial.  Expand \(G(A)G(B)\) and group the
terms by \(t=x+y\).  The \(t=0\) contribution is
\[
 \sum_{x\ne0}A(x)B(-x)
 =B(-1)\sum_{x\ne0}(AB)(x)=0.
\]
For \(t\ne0\), write \(x=tu\) and \(y=t(1-u)\).  This is a
bijection between the allowed pairs and \(t\ne0\), \(u\ne0,1\).
Consequently
\[
 G(A)G(B)
 =\sum_{t\ne0}(AB)(t)\psi(t)
       \sum_{u\ne0,1}A(u)B(1-u)
 =G(AB)J(A,B).
\]
Taking moduli and using the Gauss-sum result proves
\(|J(A,B)|=\sqrt Q\).
Finally, if \(B=A^{-1}\), the substitution
\(v=u/(1-u)\) is a bijection from
\(\mathbb F_Q\setminus\{0,1\}\) to
\(\mathbb F_Q^\times\setminus\{-1\}\), with inverse
\(u=v/(1+v)\).  Therefore
\[
 J(A,A^{-1})=\sum_{v\ne0,-1}A(v)=-A(-1).
\]
This also covers characteristic two.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:character-sum-external}
Let \(q_0=p^r\), \(Q=q_0^n\), and let
\(\ket{\psi_j}\), \(1\le j\le Q-2\), be the nontrivial Fourier
eigenvectors of Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-power-cycle}.  Use the finite-field
Weyl operators
\[
 X_v\ket{x}=\ket{x+v},\qquad
 Z_w\ket{x}=
 \exp\!\left[\frac{2\pi i}{p}
     \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_{q_0}/\mathbb F_p}(w\cdot x)
     \right]\ket{x},\qquad
 W_{v,w}=X_vZ_w,
\]
where \(x,v,w\in\mathbb F_{q_0}^n\).  For \((v,w)\ne(0,0)\),
\begin{equation}
 \left|\bra{\psi_j}W_{v,w}\ket{\psi_{j'}}\right|
 \le c_Q:=\frac{2\sqrt Q}{Q-1}
 \le\frac4{\sqrt Q}.
 \label{eq:character-sum-cQ}
\end{equation}
This holds for every prime-power \(q_0\), including characteristic two.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Identify \(\mathbb F_{q_0}^n\) with \(\mathbb F_Q\) using the basis
\(b_i=\alpha^i\), \(0\le i<n\), from
Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-power-cycle}.  Let \(b_i^\vee\) be the dual basis
for the trace pairing,
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_{q_0}}
       (b_i^\vee b_k)=\delta_{ik}.
\]
For a vector \(w\), put \(\beta_w=\sum_iw_i b_i^\vee\).
The phase of \(Z_w\) becomes the additive character
\[
 \psi_w(x)=\exp\!\left[
       \frac{2\pi i}{p}
       \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_Q/\mathbb F_p}(\beta_wx)
       \right].
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:character-trace-pairing} gives this identity and shows that \(\psi_w\) is nontrivial whenever \(w\ne0\).
In particular, this argument does not require \(p\nmid n\).

Let \(L=Q-1\) and choose the multiplicative character \(\chi\) with
\(\chi(\alpha)=e^{2\pi i/L}\).  Taking the first point of the nonzero
cycle to be \(1\), we have
\[
 \ket{\psi_j}=\frac1{\sqrt L}
       \sum_{x\in\mathbb F_Q^\times}\chi(x)^j\ket{x}.
\]
Changing the starting point of the cycle only changes the overall phase
of each eigenvector.  Write \(a\in\mathbb F_Q\) for the field element
corresponding to \(v\).  Direct substitution gives
\begin{equation}
 \bra{\psi_j}W_{v,w}\ket{\psi_{j'}}
 =\frac1L\sum_{\substack{x\in\mathbb F_Q\\x\ne0,-a}}
       \chi(x)^{j'}\chi(x+a)^{-j}\psi_w(x).
 \label{eq:prime-power-character-reduction}
\end{equation}

If \(a=0\), then \(w\ne0\).  The numerator is the Gauss sum of
\(\chi^{j'-j}\) and the nontrivial additive character \(\psi_w\).
It has modulus \(\sqrt Q\) when \(j\ne j'\), and equals \(-1\)
when \(j=j'\).

If \(a\ne0\) and \(w=0\), the change of variable \(x=-ay\) gives,
up to a factor of modulus one, the Jacobi sum
\[
 J(\chi^{j'},\chi^{-j})
 =\sum_{y\ne0,1}\chi(y)^{j'}\chi(1-y)^{-j}.
\]
Both multiplicative characters are nontrivial.  Its modulus is
\(\sqrt Q\) if \(j\ne j'\), and one if \(j=j'\).
The required Gauss and Jacobi identities were proved in
Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-gauss-jacobi}.

It remains to consider \(a\ne0\) and \(w\ne0\).  We use the mixed
character-sum bound for a degree-one additive polynomial and a rational
multiplicative argument with two distinct finite zeros or poles
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{CochranePinner2006}.  To check its hypotheses
explicitly, set
\[
 h=\gcd(j,j'),\qquad
 \widetilde\chi=\chi^h,\qquad
 G(x)=\frac{x^{j'/h}}{(x+a)^{j/h}}.
\]
Extend multiplicative characters by zero at zero.  The character
\(\widetilde\chi\) is nontrivial, since
\(1\le h\le Q-2\).  The zero and pole of \(G\) are distinct and have
coprime multiplicities, so \(G\) is not a nontrivial rational-function
power, even up to multiplication by a constant.  The additive argument
is \(F(x)=x\); \(\beta_w F(x)\) has a simple pole at infinity and hence is not of
Artin--Schreier form \(R(x)^p-R(x)+c\).  In the notation of the cited
bound, \(\deg F=1\) and there are two distinct finite zeros or poles of
\(G\).  Therefore
\[
 \left|\sum_{x\ne0,-a}
       \widetilde\chi(G(x))\psi_w(x)\right|
 \le(1+2-1)\sqrt Q=2\sqrt Q.
\]
This is exactly the numerator of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:prime-power-character-reduction}.  Dividing the three
case bounds by \(L\) proves the first inequality in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:character-sum-cQ}.  The second follows from
\(Q/(Q-1)\le2\).
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The non-elementary input is the classical mixed character-sum bound;
the reduction from Weyl matrix elements to that bound is given above.
The operators here use the additive group of the finite field
\(\mathbb F_{q_0}\).  Invertible \(\mathbb F_{q_0}\)-linear
permutations preserve this Weyl basis under conjugation, as required
below.  For \(r>1\), this convention should be distinguished from the
cyclic shift-and-phase convention on \(\mathbb Z_{p^r}\).
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:moving-head-locality}
Define the gate sequence
\begin{align}
  u_t
  &=
  g_{n-1-t},
  &&0\le t\le n-2,
  \nonumber\\
  u_{n-1}
  &=
  g_0,
  \nonumber\\
  u_t
  &=
  \mathbbm{1},
  &&n\le t\le2n-2.
  \label{eq:moving-head-sequence}
\end{align}
Its period is
\[
  K=2n-1,
\]
and its Floquet unitary is \(U_F\).  The associated periodic
Feynman--Kitaev Hamiltonian admits a static geometrically local
realisation on a strip of bounded width, with bounded-range terms and
bounded interaction degree for fixed \(q_0\).
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
By Eq.~\eqref{eq:moving-head-sequence}, the chronological nonidentity
gates are
\[
  g_{n-1},g_{n-2},\ldots,g_1,g_0.
\]
The Floquet product, with later gates multiplying on the left, is
therefore
\[
  u_{K-1}\cdots u_0
  =
  g_0g_1\cdots g_{n-1}
  =
  U_F
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:companion-staircase}.  The number of time steps is
\[
  n+(n-1)=2n-1.
\]

For locality, place the \(n\) data sites on one horizontal row.  During
the first \(n\) clock steps, place consecutive clock sites on a second row
so that the hopping edge \((t,t+1)\) lies adjacent to the one- or
two-site support of \(u_t\).  The gates \(g_{n-1},\ldots,g_1\) move
successively along neighbouring data bonds and \(g_0\) acts on the end
site.  During the remaining \(n-1\) identity steps, return the clock path
on a third adjacent row, and place its final site adjacent to the initial
clock site.  Hence the periodic closing edge also has bounded geometric
range.  Consecutive clock sites are therefore a bounded distance apart,
every controlled hopping term
\[
  u_t\otimes\ket{t+1}\!\bra t+\mathrm{h.c.}
\]
has support of bounded diameter, and each data or clock site belongs to
only a bounded number of terms.  Since \(q_0\) is fixed, all local Hilbert
spaces have fixed dimension.  This gives the claimed bounded-width local
strip.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:prime-power-static-spectrum}
For the \(K\)-step moving-head clock, every regular Floquet phase
Eq.~\eqref{eq:prime-power-phases} produces static energies
\begin{equation}
  E_{m,q}
  =
  1-
  \cos\left[
  \frac{2\pi}{KL}(mL+q)
  \right],
  \qquad
  0\le m<K,
  \quad
  1\le q<L.
  \label{eq:prime-power-static-spectrum}
\end{equation}
Thus the regular energies are a subset of the
\(KL\)-point cosine grid.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
For a general \(K\)-step periodic clock and Floquet eigenvector
\[
  U_F\ket\phi=e^{i\phi}\ket\phi,
\]
define
\[
  U_{t:0}
  =
  u_{t-1}\cdots u_0,
  \qquad
  \ket{K_{t,\phi}}
  =
  U_{t:0}\ket\phi\otimes\ket t.
\]
The periodic boundary is
\[
  \ket{K_{K,\phi}}
  =
  e^{i\phi}\ket{K_{0,\phi}}.
\]
For \(m=0,\ldots,K-1\), choose
\[
  \theta_{m,\phi}
  =
  \frac{2\pi m}{K}-\frac{\phi}{K}
\]
and
\[
  \ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}
  =
  \frac1{\sqrt K}
  \sum_{t=0}^{K-1}
  e^{i\theta_{m,\phi}t}
  \ket{K_{t,\phi}}.
\]
Exactly as in the direct calculation in
Proposition~\ref{prop:clock-spectrum}, the periodic-clock Hamiltonian acts
as the nearest-neighbour twisted Laplacian on this Krylov basis:
\[
  H_{\rm FK}\ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}
  =
  (1-\cos\theta_{m,\phi})
  \ket{\Psi_{m,\phi}}.
\]
For
\[
  \phi=\phi_q=-\frac{2\pi q}{L},
\]
one obtains
\[
  \theta_{m,q}
  =
  \frac{2\pi}{KL}(mL+q),
\]
which proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:prime-power-static-spectrum}.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:prime-power-static-matrix}
Let \(O_a\) be a nonidentity local Weyl basis operator on a fixed set of
data sites, extended trivially to the clock.  For every pair of regular
static-clock eigenstates,
\begin{equation}
  \left\lvert
  \bra{\Psi_{m,q}}
  O_a\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{\rm clock}
  \ket{\Psi_{m',q'}}
  \right\rvert
  \le
  c_Q
  \label{eq:prime-power-static-matrix}
\end{equation}
with \(c_Q\) from
Eq.~\eqref{eq:character-sum-cQ}.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Clock orthogonality gives
\begin{align}
  &\bra{\Psi_{m,q}}
  O_a\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{\rm clock}
  \ket{\Psi_{m',q'}}
  \nonumber\\
  &\qquad=
  \frac1K
  \sum_{t=0}^{K-1}
  e^{i(\theta_{m',q'}-\theta_{m,q})t}
  \bra{\psi_q}
  U_{t:0}^\dagger O_aU_{t:0}
  \ket{\psi_{q'}}.
  \label{eq:prime-power-clock-average}
\end{align}
Every gate \(g_i\) is an invertible linear permutation over
\(\mathbb F_{q_0}\).  Conjugation by such a Clifford permutation maps a
Weyl operator to another Weyl operator, and an invertible conjugation
cannot map a nonidentity operator to the identity.  Thus every
\(U_{t:0}^\dagger O_aU_{t:0}\) is a nonidentity Weyl operator.
Theorem~\ref{thm:character-sum-external} bounds every summand in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:prime-power-clock-average} by \(c_Q\) in modulus.  The
triangle inequality proves the result.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:prime-power-improved-full}
For every fixed prime-power local dimension \(q_0\) and every fixed
data subsystem \(S\), the following bounds hold for
\(0<\delta\le1\) and \(T\ge1\), respectively:
\begin{align}
  \chi_S(\delta;H_{\rm FK}^{(q_0)})
  &=
  O_{q_0}\left(
  K\delta\log\frac e\delta
  \right)
  +
  O_{q_0}(q_0^{-n}),
  \label{eq:prime-power-chi-full}\\
  \sup_{t_0,\rho_S}
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{d}
  \right)^2dt
  &=
  O_{S,q_0}\left(
  \frac{K\log(eT)}{T}
  \right)
  +
  O_{S,q_0}(q_0^{-n}).
  \label{eq:prime-power-window-full}
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  T_K
  =
  O_{\alpha,q_0}
  \left(
  K^{1+\alpha}\log K
  \right)
  \label{eq:prime-power-T-full}
\end{equation}
is sufficient for mean-square error \(O(K^{-\alpha})\).
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-power-cycle}, the exceptional Floquet dimension is
\[
  r_F=2.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-static-spectrum}, the regular static
energies have lifted grid labels with \(L=Q-1\le Q\).
The regular Floquet labels \(1,\ldots,Q-2\) are pairwise distinct,
so the injectivity hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:general-clock} holds.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:prime-power-static-matrix} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:character-sum-external},
\[
  c_Q=O_{q_0}(Q^{-1/2}).
\]
Thus the simplified form of
Theorem~\ref{thm:general-clock} applies and gives
Eq.~\eqref{eq:prime-power-chi-full}, because
\[
  Q^{-1}=q_0^{-n}.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:prime-power-window-full} follows by setting
\(\delta=T^{-1}\) in the local-band theorem.  Finally, for
\[
  T_K=K^{1+\alpha}\log(eK),
\]
one has
\[
  \frac{K\log(eT_K)}{T_K}
  =
  O_\alpha(K^{-\alpha}),
\]
while \(q_0^{-n}\) is exponentially small in
\(K=2n-1\).  This proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:prime-power-T-full}.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:FK-energy-orthogonal-new}
For any periodic Feynman--Kitaev Hamiltonian of the form
Eq.~\eqref{eq:FK} with at least two clock positions, and every
spin-only subsystem \(S\),
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf P_S
  \left(
  H_{\rm FK}
  -
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} H_{\rm FK}}{D}\mathbbm{1}
  \right)
  =
  0.
  \label{eq:FK-energy-orthogonal-new}
\end{equation}
Thus the conserved total-energy direction is exactly orthogonal to the
traceless spin-local operator algebra.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Let the bath contain all spins outside \(S\) and the full one-particle
clock space.  Every clock hopping term contains
\(\ket{t+1}\!\bra t\) or its adjoint, whose trace on the clock space is
zero.  Therefore the partial trace of all hopping terms over the clock
vanishes.  The identity term gives
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}_BH_{\rm FK}=m\mathbbm{1}_S.
\]
For the same reason every hopping term has zero full trace, so
\[
  \operatorname{Tr} H_{\rm FK}=D.
\]
The explicit projection formula from
Lemma~\ref{lem:local-projection} is
\[
  \mathsf P_S(X)
  =
  \left[
  \frac1m\operatorname{Tr}_BX
  -
  \frac{\operatorname{Tr} X}{D}\mathbbm{1}_S
  \right]\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B.
\]
Apply it to \(X=H_{\rm FK}\) and substitute the two trace identities.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:clock-factorisation-new}
In the physical second-quantized clock realisation,
\[
  N_c=\sum_t c_t^\dagger c_t
\]
commutes with \(H_{\rm FK}\).  In the invariant sector \(N_c=1\), a
spin-only subsystem factors as
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal H^{(1)}
  =
  \mathcal H_S
  \otimes
  \left(
  \mathcal H_{B_s}
  \otimes
  \mathcal H_{\rm clock}^{(1)}
  \right).
  \label{eq:clock-factorisation-new}
\end{equation}
The bath state used in all preceding theorems is therefore exactly
\begin{equation}
  \tau_B
  =
  \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{B_s}}{\dim\mathcal H_{B_s}}
  \otimes
  \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{\rm clock}^{(1)}}{K},
  \label{eq:clock-bath-new}
\end{equation}
where \(K\) is the clock length.  Every product input
\(\rho_S\otimes\tau_B\) has the same mean energy as the maximally mixed
state in the sector.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
Each hopping term in the second-quantized clock contains one clock
creation and one clock annihilation operator, so it preserves clock
particle number.  The identity term also preserves it.  Hence
\[
  [H_{\rm FK},N_c]=0.
\]
In the sector containing exactly one clock particle, the clock Hilbert
space is the \(K\)-dimensional span of the one-particle position states
\(\{\ket t\}_{t=0}^{K-1}\).  If \(S\) contains only data spins, the
remaining data spins and the entire one-particle clock belong to the
bath, which proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:clock-factorisation-new} and the
maximally mixed bath formula
Eq.~\eqref{eq:clock-bath-new}.

Finally,
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}[
  H_{\rm FK}(\rho_S\otimes\tau_B)]
  =
  \operatorname{Tr}\left[
  \rho_S
  \frac1m\operatorname{Tr}_BH_{\rm FK}
  \right].
\]
The proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:FK-energy-orthogonal-new} gives
\[
  \frac1m\operatorname{Tr}_BH_{\rm FK}=\mathbbm{1}_S.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho_S=1\), the mean energy equals \(1\) for every local
input.  The maximally mixed state in the one-particle sector has the same
mean energy because \(\operatorname{Tr} H_{\rm FK}/D=1\).
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
If clock sites themselves are split between system and bath, the fixed
one-clock-particle sector is a direct sum of local charge sectors rather
than a tensor product across that spatial cut.  The preparation
\(\rho_S\otimes\tau_B\) used throughout these notes then does not have the
assumed tensor-product form.  All explicit clock theorems therefore refer
to fixed spin-only subsystems.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:bad-time-fraction-new}
Let \(f(t)\ge0\).  If
\[
  \frac1T
  \int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}f(t)^2dt
  \le E_T,
\]
then for every \(\eta>0\),
\begin{equation}
  \frac1T
  \operatorname{meas}
  \left\{
  t\in[t_0,t_0+T]:
  f(t)\ge\eta
  \right\}
  \le
  \frac{E_T}{\eta^2}.
  \label{eq:bad-time-fraction-new}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
On the set where \(f(t)\ge\eta\), one has
\(f(t)^2\ge\eta^2\).  Therefore
\[
  E_T
  \ge
  \frac{\eta^2}{T}
  \operatorname{meas}\{t\in[t_0,t_0+T]:f(t)\ge\eta\}.
\]
Rearrange.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:quasilinear-fixed-accuracy-new}
For the binary LFSR clock, fix a trace-distance tolerance
\(\eta\in(0,1)\) and a tolerated bad-time fraction
\(\zeta\in(0,1)\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\),
\begin{equation}
  T
  =
  O_S\left(
  \frac{n}{\eta^2\zeta}
  \log\frac{en}{\eta^2\zeta}
  \right)
  \label{eq:quasilinear-window-new}
\end{equation}
is sufficient to guarantee, uniformly in the window starting time and in
the local input,
\begin{equation}
  \frac1T
  \operatorname{meas}
  \left\{
  t\in[t_0,t_0+T]:
  D_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(
  \Phi_t(\rho_S),\frac{\mathbbm{1}_S}{2^s}
  \right)
  \ge\eta
  \right\}
  \le\zeta.
  \label{eq:quasilinear-bad-new}
\end{equation}
For fixed \(\eta,\zeta\), this is \(T=O_S(n\log n)\).
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:LFSR-direct-T} gives
\[
  E_T
  \le
  C_S
  \left[
  \frac{n\log(eT)}{T}
  +
  2^{-n}
  \right].
\]
Choose
\[
  T
  =
  C\frac{n}{\eta^2\zeta}
  \log\frac{en}{\eta^2\zeta}
\]
with \(C\) large enough, depending only on \(S\), that the first term is
at most \(\eta^2\zeta/2\).  For sufficiently large \(n\), the
exponential term is also at most \(\eta^2\zeta/2\).  Hence
\(E_T\le\eta^2\zeta\).  Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:bad-time-fraction-new}.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The physical spin--clock Hamiltonians are static and geometrically local,
but their one-clock-particle sectors are exactly solvable and decompose
into Floquet-labelled tight-binding sectors.  The explicit clock theorems
are therefore not generic interacting-Hamiltonian theorems.  Their role is
to demonstrate rigorously that locally accessible spectral
anti-concentration can coexist with exponentially fine microscopic
spectral structure.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:structured-scope}
The terms \(h_i=V^\dagger D_iV\) have norm at most one and commute
pairwise.  Each is supported on at most five adjacent patches.  A fixed
physical qubit belongs to at most five such term supports.
Every operator
\[
 \Pi_{i,z}=V^\dagger
       \left(\ket z\!\bra z_i\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{\bar i}\right)V
\]
commutes with \(H_N\).  Thus the model has fixed on-site qubit dimension,
\(O(\xi)\)-body interactions of range \(O(\xi)\), and an extensive
commuting algebra of conserved operators.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Unitary conjugation preserves operator norm, and
\(\|D_i\|_\infty\le1\).  Since \(D_i,D_j\) act on disjoint tensor
factors,
\[
 [h_i,h_j]=V^\dagger[D_i,D_j]V=0.
\]
Conjugation by one matching layer can enlarge the support of an operator
only by adding patches paired to its present support.  After two layers,
an operator initially on patch \(i\) has support within
\(\{i-2,i-1,i,i+1,i+2\}\cap\{1,\ldots,M\}\).
Conversely, patch \(j\) can belong to the support of \(h_i\) only if
\(|i-j|\le2\); at most five indices satisfy this.  The same conjugation
argument applies to \(\Pi_{i,z}\), and its unconjugated form commutes with
every \(D_j\).  More explicitly, the \(N\) operators
\(Q_j=V^\dagger Z_jV\), where \(Z_j\) is the Pauli operator at
physical site \(j\), commute with one another and with \(H_N\).
Unitary invariance gives
\(D^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(Q_jQ_k)=D^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(Z_jZ_k)=\delta_{jk}\),
so there are \(N\) independent conserved directions.  This proves
the stated extensivity.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
``Bounded incidence'' here counts Hamiltonian terms containing a qubit;
it does not assert a bounded number of other qubits in each interaction.
For a local observable \(O\), terms \(h_i\) initially disjoint from its
support commute with \(O\) and with all other \(h_j\).  In the product
\(e^{itH}Oe^{-itH}\), their two exponential factors can therefore be
brought next to \(O\) and canceled.  Only terms initially overlapping
\(O\) contribute.  For a fixed-size subsystem their union has
\(O(\xi)\) qubits, independently of time.  Local relaxation in this
model does not establish transport through an extended noncommuting
chain.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:Cui-design-input}
                                                                
                                                                      
There is a universal constant \(C_0\) such that, for the ensemble
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nearly-local-H} with the reference uniform energy law,
\begin{equation}
 \xi\ge2\log_2(2N/\varepsilon)+C_0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \left\|\mathcal M_{\{e^{-i\pi H_N}\}}^{(2)}
       -\mathcal M_{\rm Haar}^{(2)}\right\|_\diamond\le\varepsilon.
 \label{eq:reference-design-condition}
\end{equation}
This is the \(k=2\), exact-Haar-gate specialization of Theorem 3 of
Ref.~\cite{CuiSchusterMaoHuangBrandao2025}.  At time \(\pi\),
independent uniform energies on \([-1,1]\) give independent uniform
phases on the unit circle.  The source's measurable-error conclusion
implies the additive-error conclusion used here.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:admissible-patches}
For every fixed \(b>0\), there are arbitrarily large system sizes
\(N=M\xi\), with \(M\) even, \(\xi=O_b(\log N)\), satisfying
Eq.~\eqref{eq:reference-design-condition} with
\(\varepsilon=N^{-b}\).
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
Let \(M\) run over sufficiently large even integers and choose
\[
 \xi=\left\lceil4(1+b)\log_2 M+C_0+2\right\rceil,\qquad N=M\xi.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(M\), \(\xi\le M\): the ratio
\(\log M/M\) tends to zero, as follows for example from
\(\log x=\int_1^x u^{-1}du\le2\sqrt x\) for \(x\ge1\).
It follows that \(\log_2N\le2\log_2M\).  Hence
\[
 2\log_2(2N/N^{-b})+C_0
 =2+2(1+b)\log_2N+C_0
 \le 4(1+b)\log_2M+C_0+2
 \le\xi.
\]
Also \(\xi=O_b(\log M)=O_b(\log N)\), and \(N\) is unbounded.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:haar-two-copy-audited}
Let \(F\) swap the two copies of \(\mathbb C^D\), where \(D\ge2\).
For every operator \(X\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal M_{\rm Haar}^{(2)}(X)
 =\frac{D\operatorname{Tr} X-\operatorname{Tr}(FX)}{D(D^2-1)}\,\mathbbm{1}
  +\frac{D\operatorname{Tr}(FX)-\operatorname{Tr} X}{D(D^2-1)}\,F.
 \label{eq:haar-two-copy-audited}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Haar invariance implies that the twirled operator commutes with
\(U\otimes U\) for every unitary \(U\).
We verify that this commutant is spanned by \(\mathbbm{1},F\).
Commutation with all diagonal phase matrices implies that its matrix
element \(\langle ij|Z|kl\rangle\) vanishes unless the multisets
\(\{i,j\}\) and \(\{k,l\}\) coincide.  To see this, vary each diagonal
phase independently; any nonzero difference of its two multiplicities
would change that matrix element by a nontrivial phase.
Commutation with all permutation matrices then makes all coefficients
of each of the three remaining types equal.  Consequently
\[
 Z=b\mathbbm{1}+cF+(a-b-c)\sum_i\ket{ii}\!\bra{ii}.
\]
A unitary taking \(\ket1\) to
\(\ket+=(\ket1+\ket2)/\sqrt2\) must take the eigenvector \(\ket{11}\),
of eigenvalue \(a\), to an eigenvector \(\ket{++}\) of the same
eigenvalue.  The coefficient of \(\ket{12}\) in \(Z\ket{++}\) is
\((b+c)/2\), while that in \(a\ket{++}\) is \(a/2\).
Thus \(a=b+c\), proving the commutant assertion.

Write the twirl as \(\alpha\mathbbm{1}+\beta F\).  Unitary invariance of trace,
and \(F(U\otimes U)=(U\otimes U)F\), give
\[
 D^2\alpha+D\beta=\operatorname{Tr} X,\qquad
 D\alpha+D^2\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(FX).
\]
Solving these two equations gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:haar-two-copy-audited}.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:design-suppresses-phi}
Let \(S\) consist of \(s\ge1\) qubits, \(d=2^s\), \(q=d^2-1\),
and let \(O_1,\ldots,O_q\) be its embedded nonidentity Pauli basis.
Define
\[
 \varphi_S(U)=\frac1q\sum_a c_a(U),\qquad
 c_a(U)=D^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(O_aUO_aU^\dagger).
\]
If \(\mathcal U\) has additive two-design error at most \(\varepsilon\),
then
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E_{\mathcal U}|\varphi_S(U)|^2
 &\le \frac1{q(D^2-1)}+\varepsilon,\label{eq:design-suppresses-phi}\\
 \left|\mathbb E_{\mathcal U}\varphi_S(U)\right|
 &\le\varepsilon.\label{eq:design-controls-first}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Every \(c_a(U)\) is real because conjugating its trace and cycling the
two Hermitian factors leaves it unchanged.  Therefore the correct
two-copy representation is
\begin{equation}
 |\varphi_S(U)|^2
 =\frac1{q^2D^2}\sum_{a,b}
   \operatorname{Tr}\!\left[
    (O_a\otimes O_b)U^{\otimes2}
    (O_a\otimes O_b)U^{\dagger\otimes2}\right].
 \label{eq:correct-two-copy-contraction}
\end{equation}
For each pair \(a,b\),
\(\|O_a\otimes O_b\|_\infty=1\) and
\(\|O_a\otimes O_b\|_1=D^2\).
The two-design norm bound therefore changes the expectation of each
normalized summand by at most \(\varepsilon\).  Indeed,
\(|\operatorname{Tr} XY|\le\|X\|_\infty\|Y\|_1\): writing a singular-value
decomposition \(Y=\sum_j s_j\ket{u_j}\!\bra{v_j}\) bounds the trace by
\(\sum_j s_j|\langle v_j|X|u_j\rangle|
 \le\|X\|_\infty\sum_j s_j\).
Averaging over \(q^2\) pairs preserves the same error bound.

For the Haar value, \(\operatorname{Tr}(O_a\otimes O_b)=0\) and
\(\operatorname{Tr}[F(O_a\otimes O_b)]=\operatorname{Tr}(O_aO_b)=D\delta_{ab}\).
Using Eq.~\eqref{eq:haar-two-copy-audited} and contracting again with
\(O_a\otimes O_b\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E_{\rm Haar}c_a(U)c_b(U)=\frac{\delta_{ab}}{D^2-1}.
\]
Summation over \(a,b\) gives the Haar value \(1/[q(D^2-1)]\).

For the first moment, use instead
\[
 c_a(U)=D^{-2}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[
 (O_a\otimes\mathbbm{1})U^{\otimes2}(O_a\otimes\mathbbm{1})U^{\dagger\otimes2}\right].
\]
The same norm estimate bounds its design error by \(\varepsilon\).
Both \(\operatorname{Tr}(O_a\otimes\mathbbm{1})\) and
\(\operatorname{Tr}[F(O_a\otimes\mathbbm{1})]\) vanish, so its Haar expectation is zero.
Averaging over \(a\) proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:design-controls-first}.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:structural-frequencies}
The weights satisfy \(W_\ell\ge0\) and \(\sum_\ell W_\ell=1\), and
\begin{equation}
 \varphi_S(t;J,V)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal I}
           W_\ell(V)e^{-it\ell\cdot J}.
 \label{eq:structured-phi}
\end{equation}
If the \(J_{i,u}\) are independent and absolutely continuous, then outside
a probability-zero set, all frequencies with different vectors \(\ell\)
are distinct, and only \(\ell=0\) has frequency zero.  On this event
\begin{align}
 \pi_{0,S}(J,V)&=W_0(V),\\
 \widetilde\varphi_S(t;J,V)
     &=\sum_{\ell\ne0}W_\ell(V)e^{-it\ell\cdot J},\\
 \overline{|\varphi_S|^2}&=\beta(V).
 \label{eq:structural-zero-and-plateau}
\end{align}
No assumption of nondegenerate ordered energy gaps is made.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
For each \(a\), summing squared matrix entries of \(VO_aV^\dagger\)
gives \(\operatorname{Tr}(O_a^\dagger O_a)=D\).  Thus the pair weights sum to one.
Expanding the normalized trace in the eigenbasis gives the pair
representation of \(\varphi_S\), and grouping pairs with equal vectors
gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:structured-phi}.

For \(\ell\ne\ell'\), choose a coordinate on which their difference is
nonzero.  Conditional on all other energies,
\((\ell-\ell')\cdot J=0\) fixes at most one value of that energy.
Absolute continuity makes its conditional probability zero.
There are finitely many pairs of vectors, so the union of these events
also has probability zero.  The same argument with \(\ell'=0\)
excludes additional zero frequencies.
The temporal identities now follow from
Lemma~\ref{lem:Cesaro-orthogonality}.  Distinct ordered pairs can still
have the same vector \(\ell\); their structural resonances have already
been included in \(W_\ell\).
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:reference-collision}
For fixed \(V\), let the superscript ``ref'' denote expectation over the
independent uniform energy law.  Then
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E_J^{\rm ref}|\varphi_S(\pi;J,V)|^2&=\beta(V),\\
 \mathbb E_J^{\rm ref}\varphi_S(\pi;J,V)&=W_0(V).
 \label{eq:reference-collision-identities}
\end{align}
Consequently, under Eq.~\eqref{eq:reference-design-condition},
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_V\beta(V)\le b_N,\qquad
 \mathbb E_VW_0(V)\le\varepsilon,\qquad
 b_N:=\varepsilon+\frac1{q(D^2-1)}.
 \label{eq:plateau-design-bound}
\end{equation}
These conclusions about \(V\) remain valid when the actual energy
distribution is changed.
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
For an integer \(k\) and \(J\) uniform on \([-1,1]\),
\[
 \mathbb E e^{-itkJ}=
 \begin{cases}\sin(kt)/(kt),&kt\ne0,\\1,&kt=0.\end{cases}
\]
At \(t=\pi\) this equals zero for nonzero \(k\).
Independence applied to Eq.~\eqref{eq:structured-phi} leaves just
\(\ell=0\) in the first moment.  In its squared modulus it leaves just
\(\ell=\ell'\), because all vector differences are integer.
This proves both identities.  Average over \(V\), apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:Cui-design-input} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:design-suppresses-phi}, and note \(W_0\ge0\).
The last assertion holds because \(W_\ell,\beta\) are functions of \(V\)
alone, not of any energy variables.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounded-density-fourier}
Suppose a random energy has a probability density \(p\) on \([-1,1]\)
which is absolutely continuous there, with derivative in \(L^1\).
If
\[
 |p(-1)|+|p(1)|+\int_{-1}^{1}|p'(x)|dx\le L_0,
\]
then its characteristic function \(g(u)=\int_{-1}^{1}p(x)e^{-iux}dx\)
satisfies
\[
 |g(u)|\le\min\{1,L_0/|u|\}\quad(u\ne0).
\]
The uniform density has \(L_0=1\).
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
The bound by one follows from nonnegativity and normalization of \(p\).
For \(u\ne0\), integration by parts gives
\[
 g(u)=\left[\frac{p(x)e^{-iux}}{-iu}\right]_{-1}^{1}
       +\frac1{iu}\int_{-1}^{1}p'(x)e^{-iux}dx.
\]
Taking absolute values proves the stated estimate.
For \(p=1/2\), the boundary terms sum to one and the derivative vanishes.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:scalar-dephasing}
Let all energies be independent, independent of \(V\), and have densities
satisfying Lemma~\ref{lem:bounded-density-fourier} with a common fixed
\(L_0\ge1\).  Put
\[
 r_{L_0}(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&|t|\le L_0,\\
 L_0^2/t^2,&|t|>L_0.
 \end{cases}
\]
For each fixed \(V\),
\begin{align}
 \left|\mathbb E_J|\varphi_S(t)|^2-\beta(V)\right|
 &\le r_{L_0}(t)\,[1-\beta(V)],\\
 \left|\mathbb E_J|\widetilde\varphi_S(t)|^2
          -[\beta(V)-W_0(V)^2]\right|
 &\le r_{L_0}(t).
 \label{eq:scalar-dephasing}
\end{align}
In particular, under the reference-design hypotheses,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E|\varphi_S(t)|^2\le b_N+r_{L_0}(t),\qquad
 \mathbb E|\widetilde\varphi_S(t)|^2\le b_N+r_{L_0}(t).
 \label{eq:scalar-dephasing-averaged}
\end{equation}
For the uniform law this gives a remainder \(\min\{1,t^{-2}\}\).
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
Expanding Eq.~\eqref{eq:structured-phi} gives
\[
 \mathbb E_J|\varphi_S(t)|^2
 =\sum_{\ell,\ell'}W_\ell W_{\ell'}
      \prod_{i,u}g_{i,u}\bigl(t(\ell_{i,u}-\ell'_{i,u})\bigr).
\]
For \(\ell=\ell'\), the product equals one and the corresponding sum is
\(\beta(V)\).  If \(\ell\ne\ell'\), choose a patch on which
\(m_{i,u}=\ell_{i,u}-\ell'_{i,u}\) is nonzero.  Each vector satisfies
\(\sum_u\ell_{i,u}=0\), so \(\sum_um_{i,u}=0\).
Therefore at least two coordinates of \(m\) are nonzero.  These
coordinates refer to independent energy variables; each nonzero integer
has modulus at least one.  For \(|t|>L_0\), at least two factors in
the product consequently have modulus at most \(L_0/|t|\), and all
remaining factors have modulus at most one.  For \(|t|\le L_0\) every
factor has modulus at most one.  The product is thus bounded by
\(r_{L_0}(t)\) in all cases.

The coefficients \(W_\ell W_{\ell'}\) are nonnegative.  Their sum over
\(\ell\ne\ell'\) is
\((\sum_\ell W_\ell)^2-\sum_\ell W_\ell^2=1-\beta(V)\).
Taking absolute values of this finite off-diagonal sum proves the first
inequality.

For \(\widetilde\varphi_S\), use
Lemma~\ref{lem:structural-frequencies} to restrict both indices to
nonzero vectors.  The diagonal sum is \(\beta-W_0^2\); the remaining
coefficients sum to
\[
 (1-W_0)^2-(\beta-W_0^2)\le1.
\]
The identical product estimate proves the second inequality.
The exceptional probability-zero set in that lemma does not change any
expectation.  Finally average over \(V\) and use
Eq.~\eqref{eq:plateau-design-bound}.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:generic-nearly-local-AS}
Assume the reference-design condition and the independent energy-density
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:scalar-dephasing}.  Then for every \(T>0\),
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E A_S(T)&\le b_N+\frac{2L_0}{T},\\
 \mathbb E\mathcal A_S(T;H)&\le b_N+\frac{2L_0}{T},\\
 \mathbb E\mathcal F_S(T;H)&\le b_N+\frac{4L_0}{T},\\
 \mathbb E\mathscr E_H(T)
      \le\mathfrak c_d\left(b_N+\frac{4L_0}{T}\right).
 \label{eq:structured-every-window-main}
\end{align}
Moreover,
\[
 \mathbb E\pi_{0,S}\le\varepsilon,\qquad
 \mathbb E\pi_{0,S}^2\le\varepsilon.
\]
The expectation in Eq.~\eqref{eq:structured-every-window-main} is outside
both the starting-time supremum and the input supremum.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
For \(T\le L_0\), \(\int_0^T r_{L_0}(t)dt=T\le2L_0\).
For \(T>L_0\), direct integration gives
\[
 \int_0^T r_{L_0}(t)dt
 =L_0+L_0^2\left(\frac1{L_0}-\frac1T\right)
 =2L_0-\frac{L_0^2}{T}\le2L_0.
\]
All squared correlations are nonnegative and bounded by one, so
interchanging the finite time integral and expectation is justified.
Equation~\eqref{eq:scalar-dephasing-averaged} and the last integral
estimate prove the two rectangular bounds.  The triangular weight has
normalized integral one and is at most one, so the same argument with
its \(1/T\) normalization gives the third bound.
Apply Eq.~\eqref{eq:positive-kernel-full} for each individual
Hamiltonian \emph{before} taking expectation to obtain the last bound.

The zero-mode statements follow from
\(\pi_{0,S}=W_0\) almost surely,
Eq.~\eqref{eq:plateau-design-bound}, and \(0\le W_0^2\le W_0\le1\).
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:generic-nearly-local-bands}
Fix \(b,c>0\).  Choose the reference error \(\varepsilon=N^{-b}\),
logarithmic patches as in Lemma~\ref{lem:admissible-patches}, and a common
density constant \(L_0\) independent of \(N\).  At \(T_N=N^c\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E A_S(T_N)
     =O_{b,L_0}\!\left(N^{-\min\{b,c\}}\right),\qquad
 \mathbb E\mathscr E_H(T_N)
     =O_{s,b,L_0}\!\left(N^{-\min\{b,c\}}\right).
 \label{eq:structured-polynomial-rates}
\end{equation}
For every \(0<a<\min\{b,c\}\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P[\mathscr E_H(N^c)>N^{-a}]
 \le \mathfrak c_d
       \left(N^{a-b}+\frac{N^a}{q(2^{2N}-1)}
                   +4L_0N^{a-c}\right).
 \label{eq:structured-high-probability}
\end{equation}
For example, \(b=c=2\) gives expected every-window mean-square error
\(O_s(N^{-2})\), and error at most \(N^{-1}\) with failure probability
\(O_s(N^{-1})\), on windows \(N^2\).
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
Substitute \(T=N^c\), \(D=2^N\), and
\(b_N=N^{-b}+1/[q(2^{2N}-1)]\) into
Theorem~\ref{thm:generic-nearly-local-AS}.  The exponential term is
smaller than any fixed inverse power of \(N\).  Apply the elementary
Markov inequality to the nonnegative Borel random variable
\(\mathscr E_H(N^c)\), with threshold \(N^{-a}\).
Setting \(b=c=2\) and \(a=1\) gives the example.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:structured-short-time-lower}
In the structured ensemble, fix \(s\ge1\) qubits, put \(d=2^s\) and
\(a_d=1-1/d\).  Every realization satisfies, for \(T\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E_H(T)\ge\frac{a_d^3}{40s\,T}.
 \label{eq:structured-short-time-lower}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for \(\varepsilon=N^{-b}\) and \(1\le T\le N^b\),
\(\mathbb E\mathscr E_H(T)=\Theta_{s,b,L_0}(T^{-1})\) for all
sufficiently large admissible \(N\).
This lower bound records the unavoidable initial transient in a
criterion that includes the window starting at zero; it is not a
pointwise long-time lower bound.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
Choose a pure subsystem input \(\rho_S\) and
\(\rho_0=\rho_S\otimes\mathbbm{1}_B/m\).
A term whose support misses \(S\) commutes with \(\rho_0\).
There are at most \(5s\) terms meeting \(S\), each of norm at most one,
by Proposition~\ref{prop:structured-scope}.  The triangle inequality and
\(\|A X\|_1\le\|A\|_\infty\|X\|_1\) therefore give
\[
 \|[H,\rho_0]\|_1
 \le\sum_{i:\,\operatorname{supp}h_i\cap S\ne\varnothing}
                 2\|h_i\|_\infty\|\rho_0\|_1
 \le10s.
\]
Unitary evolution satisfies
\([H,\rho(t)]=e^{-itH}[H,\rho_0]e^{itH}\).
Integrating its derivative thus gives
\(\|\rho(t)-\rho_0\|_1\le10s\,t\) for \(t\ge0\).

Partial trace contracts trace norm on Hermitian differences.
For completeness, if \(X=X_+-X_-\) is its positive/negative
spectral decomposition, positivity of partial trace and the triangle
inequality give
\[
 \|\operatorname{Tr}_BX\|_1
 \le\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_BX_+)+\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_BX_-)
 =\operatorname{Tr} X_++\operatorname{Tr} X_-=\|X\|_1.
\]
Hence \(D_{\mathrm{tr}}(\Phi_t(\rho_S),\rho_S)\le5s\,t\).
The eigenvalues of \(\rho_S-\mathbbm{1}_S/d\) are \(1-1/d\) and
\(d-1\) copies of \(-1/d\), so
\(D_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho_S,\mathbbm{1}_S/d)=a_d\).
The triangle inequality yields
\[
 D_{\mathrm{tr}}(\Phi_t(\rho_S),\mathbbm{1}_S/d)\ge a_d-5s\,t.
\]
For \(0\le t\le t_*=a_d/(10s)\), this distance is at least \(a_d/2\).
Since \(t_*\le1\), the length-\(T\) window starting at zero contains this
whole interval whenever \(T\ge1\).  Its average squared error is
therefore at least \(t_*a_d^2/(4T)=a_d^3/(40sT)\).
This proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:structured-short-time-lower}.

For \(T\le N^b\), the plateau \(N^{-b}\) is at most \(1/T\).
The exponential Haar term is also at most \(1/T\) for sufficiently large
\(N\).  The upper bound in
Theorem~\ref{thm:generic-nearly-local-AS} is consequently
\(O_{s,b,L_0}(1/T)\); the lower bound just proved holds for every
realization and hence after expectation.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{cor:all-longer-windows}
For a fixed Hamiltonian, if \(\mathscr E_H(T)\le u\), then for every
\(L\ge T\), every \(t_0\ge0\), and every trace-distance tolerance
\(\eta>0\),
\begin{equation}
 \frac1L\operatorname{meas}\left\{t\in[t_0,t_0+L]:
       \sup_{\rho_S}D_{\mathrm{tr}}(\Phi_t(\rho_S),\mathbbm{1}_S/d)\ge\eta\right\}
 \le\frac{2u}{\eta^2}.
 \label{eq:common-good-times}
\end{equation}
For \(L=T\) the factor two may be omitted.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
Write \(L=kT+r\), where \(k\ge1\) is an integer and \(0\le r<T\).
Split the integral of \(e_H\) into \(k\) complete windows and a final
interval of length \(r\).  The latter integral is at most that over the
length-\(T\) window starting at the same point, because \(e_H\ge0\).
Thus the whole integral is at most \((k+1)Tu\le2Lu\).
For \(L=T\), the definition gives \(Tu\) directly.
On the set in Eq.~\eqref{eq:common-good-times}, \(e_H(t)\ge\eta^2\).
Integrating this lower bound over that set proves the claim.
No union bound over a continuum of times or states is used.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
For a specified collection \(\mathcal S_N\) of at most \(N^r\)
subsystems of a fixed maximum size, a union bound applied to
Eq.~\eqref{eq:structured-high-probability} gives the corresponding
simultaneous statement with failure probability multiplied by \(N^r\).
For threshold \(N^{-a}\), the failure probability therefore tends
to zero whenever \(\min\{b,c\}>a+r\).  The maximum subsystem size
remains fixed.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:positive-kernel-stability}
Let \(G,H\) be arbitrary finite Hamiltonians on the same Hilbert space
and suppose \(\|H-G\|_\infty\le\delta\).  For every \(T>0\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E_H(T)
 \le\mathfrak c_d\left[
       2\mathcal F_S(T;G)+\frac43\delta^2T^2\right].
 \label{eq:positive-kernel-stability}
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(G\) is drawn from the structured ensemble and
\(H=G+W_N\), with \(W_N\) an arbitrary measurable perturbation,
possibly dependent on \(G\), and
\(\|W_N\|_\infty\le\delta_N\) for every realization, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E\mathscr E_H(T)
 \le\mathfrak c_d\left[
       2b_N+\frac{8L_0}{T}+\frac43\delta_N^2T^2\right].
 \label{eq:structured-stability}
\end{equation}
The perturbation need not preserve the commuting terms or their
conserved projectors.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
For \(t\ge0\), differentiating
\(e^{-i(t-s)H}e^{-isG}\) and integrating from \(s=0\) to \(s=t\)
gives
\[
 \|e^{-itH}-e^{-itG}\|_\infty\le t\|H-G\|_\infty.
\]
For negative \(t\) apply the same argument to the adjoints.
For an operator \(O\), inserting and subtracting
\(e^{-itG}Oe^{itH}\), and using unitary invariance of the
Hilbert--Schmidt norm, gives
\[
 \|e^{-itH}Oe^{itH}-e^{-itG}Oe^{itG}\|_{2,D}
 \le2\delta |t|\,\|O\|_{2,D}.
\]
Every basis element \(O_a\) has normalized Hilbert--Schmidt norm one.
Cauchy--Schwarz in the defining trace and averaging over \(a\) therefore
give
\[
 |\varphi_S(t;H)-\varphi_S(t;G)|\le2\delta|t|.
\]
It follows that
\(|\varphi_S(t;H)|^2\le2|\varphi_S(t;G)|^2+8\delta^2t^2\).
The normalized second moment of the triangular weight is
\[
 \frac1T\int_{-T}^{T}
  \left(1-\frac{|t|}{T}\right)t^2dt
 =\frac2T\left(\frac{T^3}{3}-\frac{T^3}{4}\right)=\frac{T^2}{6}.
\]
Consequently
\(\mathcal F_S(T;H)\le
2\mathcal F_S(T;G)+(4/3)\delta^2T^2\).
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-kernel-return}, then take expectations
and use Theorem~\ref{thm:generic-nearly-local-AS}.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
At \(T=N^c\) and \(\delta_N\le N^{-v}\), the perturbation term is
\(O(N^{-2(v-c)})\); it is small when \(v>c\).
A sum of at most \(C N\) bounded local perturbations, each of norm at
most \(\lambda_N\), meets this hypothesis with
\(\delta_N=C N\lambda_N\).
Thus sufficiently small noncommuting perturbations are allowed, but
their required strength vanishes with \(N\).
This is not a theorem for generic order-one noncommuting couplings.
The uniformity in the starting time comes from the positive-kernel
certificate, not from a Duhamel estimate at the possibly enormous
starting time \(t_0\).
<!-- end remark-12 -->
